"And they shall learn war no more" — that is, to carry out enmities; so that here too you may learn that Christ was not promised mighty in war, but a peace-bringer. Either deny that these things were foretold, when they are seen before your eyes; or that they are fulfilled, when they are read; or, if you deny neither, then they will be fulfilled in him concerning whom they were foretold. For look further at the very entry and course of the calling among the nations, who from the last days approach the Creator God, not at the proselytes, whose choosing is rather from the first days. For indeed the apostles brought in this faith.

22. You have the work of the apostles too foretold. "How seasonable the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things" — not war nor evils. The psalm too answered: "Into all the earth their sound has gone out, and to the ends of the earth their voices" — namely of those carrying about the law gone forth from Sion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, so that what is written might come to pass: "All who are far from my justice have drawn near to my justice and truth." When the apostles girt themselves for this business, they renounced the elders and rulers and priests of the Jews. "Was it not above all," he says, "as preachers of another god?" And yet of the very same whose Scripture they were at that moment fulfilling. "Depart, depart," cries Isaiah, "go out from thence, and touch not the unclean thing" — blasphemy, namely, against Christ. "Go out from the midst of it" — namely of the synagogue; "be separated, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." For now, according to the things written above, the Lord had revealed his Holy One by his arm — that is, by his power, Christ — in the sight of the nations, that all the nations and the ends of the earth might see the salvation that was from God. So too, turning aside from Judaism itself, when they exchanged the bonds and burdens of the law for the liberty of the gospel, they were carrying out the psalm: "Let us burst their chains and cast off from us their yoke" — certainly after the nations were in tumult and the peoples meditated vain things; "the kings of the earth stood up, and the princes were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." What did the apostles suffer thereafter? "Every iniquity," you say, "of persecutions" — from the men of the Creator, namely, as adversaries of him whom they preached. And why does the Creator, if he was an adversary of Christ, not only foretell that his apostles should suffer this, but even reproach it? For he would neither foretell the order of another god, of whom he was ignorant, as you would have it, nor would he reproach what he himself had procured. "See how the just man perishes, and no one lays it to heart, and just men are taken away, and no one regards it. For from the face of injustice the just man has been taken away." Who, but Christ? "Come," they say, "let us take away the just man, because he is unprofitable to us." Premising this, then, and subjoining accordingly that Christ too suffered, he prophesied that his just ones equally would suffer the same — both the apostles and thereafter all the faithful — marked, namely, with that sign concerning which Ezekiel: "The Lord says to me, Pass through the midst of the gate, in the midst of Jerusalem, and set the sign Tau on the foreheads of the men." For this is the letter Tau of the Greeks, but ours, T — the figure of the cross, which he foreshowed to be in the future on our foreheads, in the true and catholic Jerusalem, in which the brothers of Christ — namely the sons of God — were to render glory to God the Father, as the twenty-first psalm sings in the person of Christ himself to the Father: "I will declare thy name to my brothers, in the midst of the Church I will sing a hymn to thee." For what was to be done today in his name and spirit, he rightly proclaimed would be done by himself. And a little below: "From thee is my praise in the great Church." And in the sixty-seventh: "In the churches bless the Lord God"; so that equally might concur the prophecy of Malachi: "My will is not in you, says the Lord, and your sacrifices I will not accept; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, even a clean sacrifice" — namely the rendering of glory, and blessing, and praise, and hymns. All which, since they are found in you too — both the sealing of foreheads, and the mysteries of the churches, and the cleanness of the sacrifices — you ought now to burst out and say that the Spirit of the Creator prophesied to your Christ.

23. Now, since with the Jews you deny that their Christ has come, recognize also their own end, which they were foretold to bring upon themselves after Christ, on account of the impiety by which they both despised and slew him. For first, from the day on which, according to Isaiah, "man cast away his abominations of gold and silver, which they had made to adore vain and noxious things" — that is, from the time when the human race, the truth made clear through Christ, cast away its idols. See whether what follows has been discharged: "For the Lord of Sabaoth has taken away from Judea and from Jerusalem, among the rest, both the prophet and the wise architect" — namely the Holy Spirit, who builds the Church, namely the temple and house and city of God. For thenceforth the grace of God ceased among them, and it was commanded to the clouds that they should not rain rain upon the vineyard Sorek — that is, the heavenly benefits, that they should not come forth to the house of Israel. For it had brought forth thorns, of which it had crowned the Lord, and not justice, but a clamour, by which it had extorted him to the cross. And thus, the dews of the spiritual gifts being withdrawn, the law and the prophets reached only to John. Then, when, with such perseverance of fury, the name of the Lord too was blasphemed through them — as it is written: "Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations" (for from them began the infamy) — and in the intervening time, from Tiberius to Vespasian, they had not understood repentance, their land was made desolate, their cities burned up, their region devoured before their own eyes by strangers, the daughter of Sion forsaken and like a watchtower in a vineyard or a hut in a cucumber-field — from that time, namely, when Israel did not know the Lord, and the people did not understand him, but forsook him, and provoked to indignation the Holy One of Israel. So too the conditional threat of the sword: "If you will not, and will not hearken to me, the sword shall devour you" — proved that it was Christ whom by not hearing they perished. He who also, in the fifty-ninth psalm, demands their dispersion from the Father: "Scatter them in thy power." Who again, through Isaiah, declaiming against their burning up, says, "Because of me these things have come upon you; you shall sleep in anguish." Quite idly, if they did not suffer these things on account of him who had pronounced that they would suffer on his account, but on account of the Christ of another god. And yet, I say, you say that the Christ of another god was driven to the cross by the virtues and powers of the Creator, as by rivals. But behold, he is shown defended by the Creator — and "the worst men were given for his burial," namely those who had asserted that it was stolen away, "and the rich for his death," namely those who had both bought the betrayal from Judas and the false testimony of the stolen corpse from the soldiers. Therefore, either these things did not befall the Jews on account of him — but you are refuted, since both the sense of the Scriptures and the outcome of events and the order of the times conspire — or, if they befell on account of him, the Creator could not have avenged any but his own Christ, intending rather to reward Judas, if they had slain the adversary of his Lord. Certainly, if the Christ of the Creator has not yet come, on whose account these things are proclaimed as about to be suffered, then when he comes they will suffer them. And where then will be the daughter of Sion to be forsaken, which today is nowhere? Where the cities to be burned, which already lie in heaps? Where the dispersion of the nation, which is already in exile? Restore the state of Judea which the Christ of the Creator may find, and then contend that another came. But truly, what kind of thing is it that, by means of his own heaven, he admitted one whom he was to slay in his own land — the more honourable and glorious region of his kingdom being violated, his very court and citadel trodden under foot? Or did he rather affect this? Plainly a jealous god — yet he conquered. Blush, you who believe in a conquered god. What will you hope from one who could not protect himself? For either he was overpowered through weakness by the virtues and men of the Creator, or through malice, that he might only fasten upon them so great a guilt by his endurance.

24. "Nay," you say, "I hope from him what he himself does for the testimony of the difference: the kingdom of God of an eternal and heavenly possession." But your Christ promises to the Jews the former state, by the restitution of their land, and, after the course of life is run, refreshment in the bosom of Abraham among the dead. A most good god, if he gives back when appeased what he had also taken away when angered! O your god, who both wounds and heals, makes evils and works peace! O god merciful even to the underworld! But concerning the bosom of Abraham in its place. As for the restitution of Judea — which the Jews themselves too, led by names of places and regions, hope for just as it is described — how an allegorical interpretation may spiritually suit it to Christ and to the Church and to its state and fruit, it would be long to pursue, and it is treated in another work, which we entitle Concerning the Hope of the Faithful; and for the present it is even idle here, because the question is not of an earthly but of a heavenly promise. For we too confess that a kingdom is promised to us on earth — but before heaven, only in another state: namely, after the resurrection, for a thousand years, in the city of divine workmanship, Jerusalem brought down from heaven, which the apostle too designates as our mother on high; and, pronouncing our citizenship — that is, our municipality — to be in the heavens, he assigns it surely to some heavenly city. This city Ezekiel too knew, and the apostle John saw. And the word of the new prophecy, which is with our faith, testifies — so that it even foretold that the effigy of the city would be present to view before its actual representation, for a sign. In short, it was lately discharged in the eastern expedition. For it is established, by heathen witnesses too, that in Judea, for forty days, in the early hours of the morning, a city hung from heaven, the whole fabric of its walls vanishing with the advance of the day, and at other times nothing near at hand. This city we say is provided by God for the receiving of the saints at the resurrection and for their refreshing with an abundance of all good things — spiritual, surely — in compensation for those which in the world we either despised or lost. Since indeed it is both just and worthy of God that there too his servants should exult where they were also afflicted in his name. This is the rationale of the heavenly kingdom; after whose thousand years — within which space is enclosed the resurrection of the saints, who rise sooner or later according to their merits — then, the destruction of the world and the conflagration of judgement being accomplished, we shall be changed in a moment into the angelic substance, namely by that putting-on of incorruption over us, and shall be translated into the heavenly kingdom; concerning which the matter is now thus handled, as though it were not proclaimed with the Creator, and on this account proves the Christ of another god, by whom first and alone it was revealed. Learn, then, henceforth, that it was both proclaimed by the Creator and is to be believed, even without proclamation, with the Creator. What does it seem to you, when the seed of Abraham, after the first promise by which it is promised to the likeness of the sand, is destined also to the pattern of the stars — are not these the auspices both of an earthly and of a heavenly arrangement? When Isaac, blessing his son Jacob, says, "May God give thee of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth" — are these not examples of a twofold indulgence? In short, here too the structure of the blessing itself is to be noticed. For concerning Jacob — who is the figure of the later and preferred people, that is, of us — the first promise is of the dew of heaven, the second of earthly fatness. For we are first invited to heavenly things, when we are torn from the world, and so afterward are found about to obtain earthly things too. And your gospel also has it: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and these things shall be added to you." But to Esau he promises an earthly blessing, and subjoins a heavenly one out of the fatness of the earth, saying, "Thy dwelling shall be also of the dew of heaven." For the arrangement of the Jews is in Esau — of sons elder by birth and later by affection — first imbued with earthly goods through the law, afterward led to heavenly things through the gospel by believing. But when Jacob dreams of a ladder fixed firm in the earth up to heaven, with some angels ascending and others descending, and the Lord leaning above — rashly, if at all, shall we interpret that by this ladder is shown a way to heaven, by which some arrive, from which others fall — established by the Lord's judgement. But why, when he awoke and was first struck with the awe of the place, did he turn to the interpretation of the dream? For when he had said, "How terrible is this place!" he says, "It is nothing else but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." For he had seen Christ the Lord, the temple of God and the gate, the same through whom heaven is entered. And surely he would not have named "the gate of heaven" if heaven is not entered with the Creator. But there is a gate too, which both receives and leads through, paved already by Christ. Of which Amos says: "Who builds his ascent into heaven" — surely not for himself alone, but for his own too, who will be with him. "For thou shalt put them about thee," he says, "as the ornament of a bride." Thus, tending through that ascent to the heavenly kingdoms, the Spirit marvels, saying, "They fly as those who are kites, as the clouds fly, and as the young of doves" — to me, namely, simply as doves. For we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, according to the apostle (that son of man, namely, coming in the clouds, according to Daniel), and so we shall ever be with the Lord — in so far as we shall be both on earth and in heaven; who, on account of the ungrateful of either promise, calls the very elements to witness: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth." And for my part, even if no hand of heavenly hope were held out to me by Scripture so often, I should have prejudice enough of this promise too, from the fact that I already hold the earthly grace; I should expect something from heaven also, from the God of heaven as well as of earth; thus I should believe that Christ, promising loftier things, belongs to him who had promised humbler ones too — who had also made trials of greater things by small ones, who had reserved the proclamation of this kingdom (unheard-of, if at all) for Christ alone, so that by his servants earthly glory should be announced, but the heavenly by God himself. But you argue from this too another Christ, because he announces a new kingdom. First you must bring forward some example of his indulgence, lest with reason I doubt the credit of so great a promise, which you say is to be hoped for; nay, before all things, that you should prove some heaven of his whom you preach to promise heavenly things. But as it is, you call to a supper and do not show the house; you allege a kingdom and do not point out the palace. Or is it because your Christ promises a heavenly kingdom while having no heaven — just as he furnished forth a man too while having no flesh? O the all-phantom! O the sleight even of so great a promise!

1. Nothing is without an origin except God alone. And as far as origin precedes in the standing of all things, so far must it precede also in their re-examination, that the standing may be established; for you cannot discern what a thing is and of what kind, unless you are certain that it is, once you have learned whence it is. And so, having come down to this subject in the order of my little work, I demand of Marcion the origin of the apostle as well — a fresh sort of disciple, the pupil of no other, who for the present believe nothing except that nothing is to be believed rashly, and that whatever is believed without acknowledgement of its origin is believed rashly. And I shall most fittingly carry this inquiry to the point of anxiety, since the man is affirmed to me as an apostle whom I do not find in the roll of the apostles in the gospel. So then, hearing that he was afterwards taken on by the Lord, when the Lord was already at rest in the heavens, I judge it a kind of improvidence that Christ did not know beforehand that this man would be necessary to him, but, once the office of the apostolate had been arranged and dismissed upon its work, thought he must be added by sudden encounter and not by foresight — by necessity, so to speak, not by will. Therefore, shipmaster of Pontus, if you have never received stolen or contraband wares into your boats, if you have never diverted or adulterated any cargo whatever — being doubtless the more cautious and faithful in the things of God — I would have you publish to us by what token you have taken on the apostle Paul, who stamped him with the mark of a title, who consigned him to you, who put him on board, that you may be able to set him forth with assurance, lest he be proved to belong to that one who has produced all the documents of his apostleship. He professed himself an apostle, you say, and indeed not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ. Plainly anyone can profess himself; but his profession is made good by another's authority: one writes, another countersigns, another seals, another enters it in the records. No one is at once witness and professor on his own behalf. Besides this you have surely read that many would come who would say, I am Christ. If there is one to lie that he is Christ, how much more one to proclaim himself an apostle of Christ? Still I am moving in the character of a disciple and an inquirer, that even from here I may blunt your faith — you who have no means of proving it — and shame your effrontery — you who lay claim, and do not take up the means by which you might lay claim. Let there be a Christ, let there be an apostle, but of that other God, so long as they are not proved except out of the instrument of the Creator. For Genesis long ago promised me Paul as well. For among those figures and prophetic blessings of Jacob upon his sons, when he had said to Benjamin, Benjamin, he says, a ravening wolf shall feed in the morning, and at evening shall give food — for he foresaw that Paul would arise from the tribe of Benjamin, a ravening wolf feeding in the morning, that is, in his early age laying waste the flock of the Lord as a persecutor of the churches, and afterwards giving food at evening, that is, in his now declining age teaching the sheep of Christ as a doctor of the nations. For the harshness too of Saul's persecution of David at first, and afterwards his repentance and amends, receiving good for evil, portended nothing else than Paul in Saul according to the tribe, and Jesus in David according to the reckoning of the virgin. If these sacraments of the figures displease you, at least the Acts of the Apostles have handed down to me this order of Paul's career, not to be denied by you either. Thence I show the apostle to have been a persecutor, not from men nor through man; thence I am induced to believe him myself; thence I expel you from his defence, and I do not fear you saying, Do you then deny the apostle Paul? I do not blaspheme him whom I protect. I deny him in order to compel you to prove him; I deny him in order to convince you that he is mine. Or if you look to our faith, accept what makes it; if you appeal to your own, produce what underpins it. Either prove that what you believe is, or, if you do not prove it, how do you believe? Or what manner of believer are you against him by whom alone is proved to be that very thing which you believe? Have now both the apostle from my side, just as the Christ also, as much my apostle as my Christ. We shall fight on these same lines here too, we shall challenge on the very step of prescription — that the apostle, namely, who is denied to the Creator, who indeed is brought forward against the Creator, must teach nothing, hold nothing, will nothing according to the Creator, and above all must proclaim another God with as great constancy as that with which he broke off from the law of the Creator. For it is not likely that, turning men away from Judaism, he should not equally have shown into the faith of what God he was turning them, since no one could pass over from the Creator without knowing to whom he was to pass. For either Christ had already revealed another God — and then the apostle's testimony followed, that he might not be reckoned the apostle of a God whom Christ had revealed, and because what had already been revealed by Christ could not be hidden from the apostle — or else Christ had revealed nothing of the kind concerning God, and then it ought all the more to have been revealed by the apostle, since now it could not be by another, and is surely not to be believed if not revealed even by the apostle. This we have established beforehand, that from here we may profess that we shall prove no other God carried about by the apostle, just as we proved none by Christ, out of Paul's own epistles, which therefore — mutilated even in their number — the very shape of the heretic's gospel ought already to have prejudged.

2. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. The epistle that teaches the Galatians we too confess to be foremost against Judaism. For we embrace that whole abolition of the old law, as itself coming from the Creator's arrangement, just as we have already often argued in this work concerning the renewal foretold by the prophets of our God. But if the Creator promised that old things should pass away, with new things, namely, about to arise, and Christ, fixing the boundary of that distinction (the law and the prophets were until John) by setting John as the terminus between either order — of the old thereafter ceasing and the new beginning — then of necessity the apostle too, in Christ revealed after John, weakens the old and confirms the new, and so concerns himself with no other faith than the Creator's, with whom the passing away of the old was also being preached. Therefore both the destruction of the law and the building up of the gospel work for me in this epistle also, belonging to that presumption of the Galatians by which they presumed that Christ was to be believed as the Creator's, with the Creator's law preserved — for it still seemed incredible that the law should be laid aside by its own author. Moreover, if they had heard at all of another God from the apostle, they would assuredly have known of their own accord that they must withdraw from the law of that God whom they had left in following another. For who would wait any longer to learn that he ought to follow a new discipline, when he had received a new God? Rather, because the same divinity was being preached in the gospel which had always been known in the law, but the discipline was not the same, this was the whole state of the question: whether the Creator's law ought to be excluded by the gospel in the Creator's Christ. Take away this state of the case, and the question is void. And the question being void, all of their own accord recognising that they must withdraw from the order of the Creator through the faith of another God, no matter would have been left for the apostle to teach this so pressingly, which the very faith would of itself have dictated. Therefore the whole intent of this epistle teaches nothing else than the withdrawal of the law coming from the Creator's arrangement, as we shall still go on to urge. If likewise he brings forward no mention of any new God — which he would nowhere have done more readily than in this matter, so as to set forth the reason for dismissing the law by this single and most sufficient definition of a new divinity — it appears how he writes: I marvel that you are so quickly transferred from him who called you into grace to another gospel: another in conduct, not in religion; in discipline, not in divinity; since the gospel of Christ ought to call them away from the law to grace, not from the Creator to another God. For no one had moved them from the Creator, so as to seem to be transferred to another gospel as while they are transferred to the Creator. For also, by adding that there was no other gospel at all, he confirms that which he maintains to be. But the Creator too promises a gospel, saying through Isaiah, Go up onto the high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Sion; lift up your voice in strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem; likewise of the person of the apostles, How timely are the feet of those bringing good tidings of peace, of those bringing good tidings of good things — to the nations also, surely; since, In his name, he says, shall the nations hope — Christ's name, to whom he says, I have set you for a light of the nations. But there is also a gospel of the new God, you say, then defended by the apostle. Then there are two gospels with two gods, and the apostle will have lied in saying that there is no other at all, when there is another, since he could so have defended his own gospel as rather to show it the one than to determine it the only one. But perhaps, to escape this point, you will say he therefore subjoined, Though an angel from heaven should preach otherwise, let him be anathema, because he knew the Creator too would preach a gospel. So again you entangle yourself. For this is what you are bound by: to confirm two gospels is not the part of one who has already denied that there is another. Yet the sense of him who set his own person first shines out: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach otherwise. For it was said by way of illustration. For the rest, if not even he himself was to preach otherwise, then surely no angel either. Thus he named an angel for this purpose, that much more should men not be believed when even an angel was not to be, nor an apostle, lest he should refer the angel to the Creator's gospel. Thereupon, running through the order of his own conversion from persecutor into apostle, he confirms the scripture of the Acts of the Apostles, in which the very subject of this epistle is also recognised: that certain men had intervened who said that men ought to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses, and that the apostles, then consulted on this question, declared on the authority of the Spirit that burdens ought not to be imposed on men which the fathers themselves had not been able to bear. But if from this too the Acts of the Apostles agree with Paul, why you reject them already appears, namely because they preach no other God than the Creator, nor a Christ of any other than the Creator's — since not even the promise of the Holy Spirit is proved to have been exhibited from any source but the instrument of the Acts. And it is surely not likely that they should agree with the apostle in part, when they show his order according to his own testimony, but disagree in part, when they announce the divinity of the Creator in Christ — so that Paul should not have followed the preaching of the apostles, from whom he received the form for unteaching the law.

3. Lastly, he writes that he went up to Jerusalem, to the patronage of Peter and of the other apostles, after fourteen years, to confer with them about the rule of his gospel, lest he should have run, or be running, in vain for so many years — that is, if he were preaching anything outside their form. So far did he desire to be approved and established by those whom, if ever, you wish to be understood as the more closely akin to Judaism. But when he says that not even Titus was circumcised, he begins to show that the question of circumcision alone was being shaken from the defence still made of the law by those whom for that reason he calls false and surreptitiously introduced brethren, men proceeding to establish nothing else than the continuance of the law, out of a faith in the Creator no doubt still intact, and so perverting the gospel — not by interpolation of the scripture, by which they would have fashioned a Christ of the Creator, but by retention of the old discipline, that they might not exclude the Creator's law. Therefore, he says, because of the false surreptitious brethren, who had crept in to spy out our liberty, which we have in Christ, that they might bring us into bondage, we did not yield to subjection even for an hour. Let us attend both to the very sense and to its cause, and the corruption of the scripture will appear. When he sends before, But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised, and then subjoins, Because of the surreptitious false brethren, and the rest, he is beginning, surely, to give the reason for a contrary act, showing on what account he did what he would neither have done nor disclosed, had not that on account of which he did it occurred. In short, I would have you say: had not those false brethren crept in to spy out their liberty, would they have yielded to subjection? I think not. Therefore they yielded, because there were those for whose sake it might be believed. For this was fitting for a faith still raw and still in suspense about the observance of the law, the apostle himself too being suspected of having run, or running, in vain. And so the false brethren had to be frustrated, as they spied out the Christian liberty, lest they should lead it into the bondage of Judaism before Paul knew that he had not run in vain, before his predecessors gave him their right hands, before from their reckoning he should take up the office of preaching among the nations. Necessarily, then, he yielded for a time; and so the reason holds for his circumcising Timothy and bringing in shaven men into the temple, which things are told in the Acts — so true that they agree with the apostle when he professes that he was made a Jew to the Jews, that he might gain the Jews, and lived under the law for the sake of those who were under the law, and so too for the sake of those surreptitiously introduced, and at last became all things to all, that he might gain all. If these things too require to be understood from this, then no one will doubt this either, that Paul was the preacher of that God and Christ whose law, though for the moment excluding it, he had yet admitted to suit the times — a law to be cast off at once, had he brought in a new God. Well, then, that Peter and James and John gave their right hands to Paul, and covenanted about the distribution of office, that Paul should go to the nations and they to the circumcision, only that they should remember the poor — and this according to the law of the Creator, who cherishes the poor and needy, as was proved in the review of your gospel. So clear is it that the question was about the law alone, while it is shown what ought to be kept out of the law. But he reproves Peter for not walking with a straight foot toward the truth of the gospel. He reproves him plainly, yet for no other reason than for the inconstancy of diet, which he varied according to the quality of persons, fearing those who were of the circumcision — not for any perversion of divinity, on account of which he would have withstood others too to their faces, he who for the lesser cause of doubtful conduct did not spare Peter himself. But how would the Marcionites have it believed? For the rest, let the apostle proceed, denying that a man is justified by works of the law, but by faith. Yet the faith of the same God whose also is the law. For he would not have laboured to distinguish faith from the law, when the diversity of the divinity itself would of its own accord have distinguished it, had there been any. With reason he did not rebuild what he had destroyed. But the law had to be destroyed from the time the voice of John cried in the wilderness, Prepare the ways of the Lord, that the rivers and hills and mountains might be filled and brought low, and the crooked and rough ways made into straightness and into plains — that is, the difficulties of the law into the facilities of the gospel. He remembered too that it was already the psalm's time: Let us break their bonds from us, and cast away their yoke from us — from the time the nations raged and the peoples imagined vain things; the kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ; so that now a man should be justified out of the liberty of faith, not out of the bondage of the law, because the just lives by faith. But if the prophet Habakkuk announced this beforehand, you have the apostle too confirming the prophets, just as Christ does. His, then, will be the faith in which the just shall live, whose also is the law, in which the worker is not justified. Accordingly, if in the law there is a curse, but in faith a blessing, you have both set forth by the Creator: Behold, he says, I have set before you a curse and a blessing. You cannot claim a distinction which, though it be of things, is therefore not of authors, since it is set forth by one author. But why Christ was made a curse for us is made plain by the very teaching of the apostle: how it agrees with us, that is, according to the faith of the Creator. For not because the Creator pronounced, Cursed is everyone hanged on a tree, will Christ therefore seem to belong to another God, and to have been on that account already then cursed in the law by the Creator. And how could the Creator have fore-cursed him whom he does not know? But why should it not rather befit the Creator to have given his own Son to his own curse, than to have subjected him to that God of yours — and that for a stranger man? In short, if this seems savage in the Creator regarding his Son, so it is in your God too; but if it is rational even in yours, so it is in mine too, and more in mine. For it would more easily be believed to be his — to have looked through the curse of Christ to a blessing for man — who had at some time set both a curse and a blessing before man, than his who has never with you professed either. We have received, then, a spiritual blessing through faith, he says — by which, namely, the just shall live, according to the Creator. This, then, is what I say, that the faith is of that God whose is the pattern of the grace of faith. But also, when he adds, For you are all sons of faith, it is shown what here above the heretic's industry has erased: the mention of Abraham, namely, by which the apostle affirms us to be sons of Abraham through faith, according to which mention he here too noted us sons of faith. For otherwise, how sons of faith? and of whose faith, if not Abraham's? For if Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, and thereafter he deserved to be named the father of many nations, while we too by believing God are likewise the more justified, like Abraham, and likewise obtain life, since the just lives by faith — so it comes about that he both above pronounced us sons of Abraham, as of the father of faith, and here sons of faith, through which Abraham had been promised the father of nations. The very point that he was recalling faith from circumcision — was he not seeking to constitute sons of Abraham, who had believed in the integrity of the flesh? In short, the faith of another God cannot be admitted to the pattern of another God, so as to reckon believers unto righteousness, to make the just live, to call the nations sons of faith. This whole thing is his with whom it is already known beforehand under the same mention of Abraham, while by the very sense he is convicted.

4. Still, he says, I speak after the manner of man: While we were children, we were placed under the elements of the world, to be in bondage to them. But this is not said in a merely human way. For it is not an illustration, but the truth. For what child — in sense, that is, such as the nations are — is not subject to the elements of the world, which it looks up to in place of God? But the human way lay in this, that, though he had said After the manner of man, yet a man's testament no one despises or overrides. For by the example of a human testament that endures, he was protecting the divine. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He did not say, To seeds, as of many, but, To his seed, as of one, which is Christ. Let Marcion's sponge blush! Unless that I review out of abundance what he has taken away, since it is the stronger thing to convict him out of what he has kept. But when it came to pass that the time was fulfilled, God sent his Son — surely he who is the God also of those very times of which the age consists, who ordained too the signs of the times, suns and moons and constellations and stars, who lastly both arranged and foretold the revelation of his Son at the extremity of the times. In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest; and, In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, according to Joel. It was for him to have waited for the time to be fulfilled, whose was also the end of time, as the beginning. But that idle God, of no operation and of no preaching, and so of no time either — what did he do at all to bring it about that the time should be fulfilled and the fulfilment awaited? If nothing, it is empty enough that he should have awaited the Creator's times, serving the Creator. And for what purpose did he send his Son? That he might redeem those who were under the law; that is, that he might make the crooked into a straight way and the rough into smooth ways, according to Isaiah, that the old should pass and the new arise, a new law out of Sion and the word of the Lord out of Jerusalem, and that we might receive the adoption of sons — the nations, namely, who were not sons. For he himself shall be a light of the nations, and in his name the nations shall hope. And so, that it might be certain that we are sons of God, he sent his Spirit into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. For in the last days, he says, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. Whose grace, except his whose is also the promise of grace? What father, except him who is also the maker? After these riches, then, there was no returning to the weak and beggarly elements. But elements, among the Romans too, the first letters are wont to be called. Not, therefore, by disparagement of the world's elements did he wish to turn them away from the God of those elements, even though by saying above, If, then, you serve those who by nature are not gods, he brands the error of natural — that is, physical — superstition, which holds the elements in place of God; yet not even so does he tax the God of the elements. But what elements he wishes understood — the first letters, namely, of the law — he himself declares. You observe days and months and seasons and years and sabbaths, I suppose, and pure suppers and fasts and great days. For to cease from these too, as from circumcision, was required by the decrees of the Creator, who also says through Isaiah, Your new moons and sabbaths and the great day I will not endure; the fast and the holidays and your ceremonies my soul hates. And through Amos, I hate, I have rejected your ceremonies, and I will not smell in your assemblies; likewise through Hosea, I will turn away all her joys and her ceremonies and her sabbaths and her new moons and all her assemblies. What he himself had appointed, you say, did he erase? Rather he than another; or if another, then that one assisted the sentence of the Creator, taking away what the Creator too had condemned. But it is not for this place to ask why the Creator broke his own laws. It is enough that we have proved that he would break them, so that it may be confirmed that the apostle determined nothing against the Creator, since the very removal of the law is from the Creator. But as something of the booty is wont to slip from thieves as evidence, so I believe Marcion too left behind the last mention of Abraham, none more to be taken away, though he turned it in part. For if Abraham had two sons, one of the handmaid, the other of the freewoman, but he who was of the handmaid was born after the flesh, while he who was of the freewoman by promise (which things are allegorical, that is, portending something else; for these are two testaments, or two displays, as we find it interpreted: one from Mount Sinai, generating into the bondage of the synagogue of the Jews according to the law, the other generating above every principality, might, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but in that to come, which is our mother, into which we have promised the holy church; and therefore he adds, Wherefore, brethren, we are not the sons of the handmaid, but of the freewoman) — assuredly he made plain that the nobility of Christianity, in the son of Abraham born of the freewoman, has the sacrament of an allegory, just as the legal bondage of Judaism in the son of the handmaid, and that so both arrangements belong to that God with whom we find the delineation of both arrangements. The very word he uses, By that liberty wherewith Christ has set us free, does it not constitute him the emancipator who had been lord? For not even Galba emancipated other men's slaves, though he would more easily set free the free. By him, therefore, will liberty be provided, with whom was the bondage of the law. And with reason. It did not befit the emancipated to be bound again by the yoke of bondage, that is, of the law, the psalm being now fulfilled: Let us break their bonds, and cast away their yoke from us, after the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. The emancipated from bondage, then, he persisted in erasing the very mark of bondage, circumcision — out of the authority, namely, of the prophetic preaching, mindful of what was said through Jeremiah, And circumcise the foreskins of your heart; for Moses too said, You shall circumcise your hardness of heart, that is, not the flesh. In short, if, coming from another God, he excluded circumcision, why does he also deny that uncircumcision avails anything in Christ, just as circumcision? For he ought to have preferred its rival, which he was assailing, had it been of a God who was circumcision's rival. But since both circumcision and uncircumcision were reckoned to one God, therefore both were of no avail in Christ, on account of the precedence of faith — that faith of which it was written, And in his name the nations shall believe; that faith which, by saying that it is perfected through love, he likewise showed to be the Creator's. For whether he means the love which is toward God — and this too is the Creator's, You shall love God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with all your strength — or the love toward one's neighbour, And your neighbour as yourself, it is the Creator's. But he that troubles you shall bear judgement. From what God? From the good one? But he does not judge. From the Creator? But neither will he condemn the asserter of circumcision. But if there shall be no other to judge but the Creator, then he will not condemn the defenders of the law except he himself who appointed that it should cease. What now, if he even confirms it in the part in which he ought? For the whole law, he says, is fulfilled in you: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Now if he wishes it understood as, It is fulfilled, as though now not to be fulfilled, then he does not wish me to love my neighbour as myself, so that this too should have ceased with the law. But we must persevere always in this precept. Therefore the law of the Creator has been approved even by the adversary, and has obtained from him not loss but compendium, its sum reduced into one precept now. But neither does this befit another more than the author. And so, when he says, Bear one another's burdens, and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ — if this cannot be done unless one love his neighbour as himself, it appears that, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, through which is heard, Bear one another's burdens, is the law of Christ, which is the Creator's, and that so Christ is the Creator's, while the law of Christ is the Creator's. You are mistaken: God is not mocked. But the God of Marcion can be mocked, who knows neither to be angry nor to avenge. For what a man sows, that also shall he reap. Therefore he holds out a God of retribution and judgement. But in doing good let us not grow weary, and while we have time, let us work good. Deny that the Creator commanded good to be done, and let the contrary doctrine be of a contrary divinity. But if he preaches retribution, from the same will come both the harvest of corruption and of life. And in his own time we shall reap, because Ecclesiastes too says, There will be a time for everything. But to me also, the servant of the Creator, the world is crucified, yet not the God of the world, and I to the world, yet not to the God of the world. For he set down the world as regards its conduct, in renouncing which we are mutually transfixed and die to one another. Persecutors he calls them of Christ. But when he adds that he bears the marks of Christ in his body (which surely are bodily things), he has now professed not a putative but a true and solid flesh of Christ, whose bodily marks he displays.

5. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. The forestructure of the former epistle so led me that I have not gone back over its heading, being certain that it can be reviewed elsewhere too — common, namely, and the same in all the epistles, in that he does not prescribe salvation to those to whom he writes, but grace and peace. I do not say what he, the destroyer of Judaism, has to do with the still Jewish custom. For even today the Jews address one another in the name of peace, and of old in the scriptures they so saluted. But I understand that he defended by his own office the preaching of the Creator: How timely the feet of those bringing good tidings of good things, of those bringing good tidings of peace. For as the evangelist of good things, that is, of the grace of God, he knew that peace was to be preferred. When, announcing these from God our Father and the Lord Jesus, he uses common names, suitable to our sacrament too, I do not think it can be discerned what God is Father, and what Lord is preached as Jesus, except from what is added, to whom they more befit. First, indeed, I prescribe that the Lord Father is to be acknowledged as no other than the Creator and founder both of man and of the universe; and further, that to the Father the name of Lord too is added on account of power, which the Son too receives through the Father; and then, that grace and peace belong not only to him from whom they were preached, but to him who had been offended. For grace is not made except after an offence, nor peace except after war. And the people, by transgression of discipline, and the whole race of man, by dissimulation of nature, had both sinned and rebelled against the Creator. But the God of Marcion, both because he is unknown could not be offended, and because he knows not to be angry. What grace, then, from one not offended? what peace from one not rebelled against? He says that the cross of Christ is foolishness to those who perish, but the power and wisdom of God to those who are to obtain salvation; and to show whence this came, he adds: For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nought the prudence of the prudent. If these are the Creator's, and he reckons among foolishness the things which pertain to the cause of the cross, then both the cross and, through the cross, Christ will pertain to the Creator, by whom was preached that which pertains to the cross. Or if the Creator, as a rival, on that account took away wisdom, that the cross of Christ his adversary might be reckoned foolishness, how can the Creator have pronounced anything pertaining to the cross of a Christ not his own, whom he did not know when he preached it? But also, why with the Lord who is supremely good and of lavish mercy do some refer salvation, believing the cross to be the power and wisdom of God, others perdition, to whom the cross of Christ is reputed foolishness — if it is not the Creator's part to have punished some offence both of the people and of the human race by the loss of wisdom and prudence? This the sequel will confirm, when he says, Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? and when here too he adds why: Since in the wisdom of God the world did not by wisdom know the Lord, God thought good to save the believers by the foolishness of preaching. But first I will dispute about the world, since the most subtle heretics here especially interpret world as the God of the world, while we understand the man who is in the world, from the simple form of human speech, by which we very often put that which contains for that which is contained. The circus cried out, and the forum spoke, and the basilica roared — that is, those who transacted business in those places. Therefore, because man, not God, in the world's wisdom did not know God, whom he ought to have known — both the Jew in the wisdom of the scriptures and every nation in the wisdom of works — therefore the same God, who was not acknowledged in his own wisdom, determined to beat back the wisdom of men with foolishness, by saving the believers, namely, in the foolish preaching of the cross. Since the Jews desire signs, who ought already to have been certain of God, and the Greeks seek wisdom, who set up their own, namely, not God's wisdom. For the rest, if a new God were being preached, in what had the Jews sinned in desiring signs by which to believe, or the Greeks in following the wisdom they should the rather believe? Thus the very recompense upon Jews and Greeks confirms both a zealous and a judging God, who from emulous retribution and as judge made foolish the wisdom of the world. But if the causes are his whose scriptures are adduced, then the apostle, treating of the Creator unknown, surely teaches that the Creator is to be known. Also, that he preaches Christ a stumbling-block to the Jews, he seals the Creator's prophecy concerning him, who says through Isaiah, Behold, I have set in Sion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence; and the rock was Christ. This Marcion too keeps. But what is the foolish thing of God wiser than men, except the cross and death of Christ? What is the weak thing of God stronger than man, except the nativity and flesh of God? But if Christ was neither born of a virgin nor framed of flesh, and through this neither truly suffered the cross nor death, there was nothing foolish and weak in him; nor did God then choose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, nor the weak things of the world to confound the strong, nor the base and least and contemptible things, which are not — that is, which are not truly — to confound the things which are, that is, which truly are. For nothing arranged by God is truly small and ignoble and contemptible, but what is by man. But with the Creator even the old things can be reckoned to foolishness and weakness and baseness and littleness and contempt. What more foolish, what weaker, than the exaction by God of bloody sacrifices and reeking holocausts? What weaker than the cleansing of little vessels and pallets? What more base than another dishonouring of the flesh already blushing? What so lowly as the prescription of retaliation? What so contemptible as the abstaining from foods? The whole Old Testament, so far as I know, every heretic derides. For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom. The God of Marcion has nothing of the kind, because he does not even emulously confute contraries with contraries, that no flesh should glory; that, as it is written, He that glories, let him glory in the Lord. In whom? Surely in him who commanded this. Unless the Creator of the precept, that one may glory in the God of Marcion.

6. By all these things, then, he shows of what God he speaks the wisdom among the perfect: of him, namely, who took away the wisdom of the wise and made void the prudence of the prudent, who made foolish the wisdom of the world, choosing its foolish things and arranging them for salvation. This wisdom he says was in secret — the wisdom which was in foolish and little and base things, which lay hidden too under figures, allegories, and riddles, to be revealed afterwards in Christ, set for a light of the nations by the Creator, who promised through the voice of Isaiah that he would lay open invisible and hidden treasures. For that the God who did nothing at all in which anything could be supposed to have been hidden should have hidden anything, is incredible enough. If he himself existed, he could not lie hidden, much less any of his sacraments. But the Creator is as well known as his sacraments, openly running their course, namely, among Israel, but overshadowed by significations, in which the wisdom of God lay concealed, to be narrated among the perfect in its own time, but set forth in the purpose of God before the ages. Whose are the ages, except the Creator's? For if the ages are built of times, and times are joined together of days and months and years, and days and months and years are marked by the suns and moons and constellations of the Creator, set by him for this (And they shall be, he says, for signs of months and years), it appears that both the ages are the Creator's, and that all that is said to have been purposed before the ages is of no other than him whose are the ages. Or let Marcion prove the ages of his God; let him show the very world too in which the ages are reckoned — a kind of vessel of times — and some signs or order of them. If he demonstrates nothing, I return to say this too: But why did he purpose our glory before the ages? It might seem that he purposed it before the ages, which he would reveal by the introduction of the age. But when he does this with almost all the ages of the Creator now run forth, he purposed it before the ages in vain, and not rather within the ages, since he was about to reveal it almost after the ages. For it is not his to have hastened in purposing whose it was also to have delayed in revealing. But to the Creator both befit: both to have purposed before the ages and to have revealed at the end of the ages, because both what he purposed and revealed he furnished beforehand, in the middle space of the ages, in figures and riddles and allegories. But because he subjoins of our glory that none of the princes of this age knew it — for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory — the heretic argues that the princes of this age crucified the Lord, the Christ, namely, of another God, that this too may fall back upon the Creator. But for him to whom we showed above in what ways our glory is to be reckoned of the Creator, it ought to be foreshown that the glory which was in secret with the Creator was rightly unknown even to all the virtues and powers of the Creator, because not even servants are permitted to know the counsels of their lords, much less those apostate angels and the very prince of transgression, the devil — whom I would contend to have been the more strangers, on account of their fault, from all consciousness of the Creator's arrangements. But now it does not even befit me to interpret the princes of this age as the virtues and powers of the Creator, because the apostle ascribes ignorance to them, whereas Jesus, even according to our gospel, the devil too knew in the temptation, and according to the common instrument the unclean spirit knew that he was the Holy One of God and was called Jesus and had come for their destruction. The parable too of the strong armed man, whom another stronger overpowered and seized his goods, if it be taken of the Creator according to Marcion, then the Creator could no longer have been ignorant of the God of glory, while he is overpowered by him, nor have nailed to the cross him against whom he could not prevail; and it remains that, according to me at least, it is credible that the virtues and powers of the Creator, knowing the God of glory, crucified him their own Christ — by that desperation and overflow of malice with which the most wicked servants too do not hesitate to slay their lords. For it is written with me that Satan entered into Judas. But according to Marcion, not even the apostle in this place suffers ignorance to be ascribed to the virtues of the Creator concerning the Lord of glory, because, namely, he does not wish them understood as the princes of this age. But if he seems not to have spoken of spiritual princes, then he spoke of secular ones — of the chief people, surely not among the nations — of its very rulers, of King Herod, of Pilate too, and of the Roman dignity, by which the greater principality of this age presided. Thus, while the argumentations of the opposite party are destroyed, our expositions are built up. But you wish further that our glory be of your God, and that it was with him in secret. And why does God and the apostle still both rely on the same instrument? What has he everywhere to do with the sentences of the prophets? For who has known the mind of the Lord, and who was his counsellor? It is Isaiah. What has he even to do with examples of our God? For when he affirms himself a prudent architect, we find this signified by the proclaimer of the divine discipline, the Creator, through Isaiah. For I will take away, he says, from Judaea, among the rest, also the wise architect. And was not Paul himself then destined — to be taken from Judaea, that is, from Judaism, unto the building of Christianity, about to lay the one foundation which is Christ? For of this too the Creator says through the same prophet, Behold, I lay in the foundations of Sion a precious stone, honourable, and he that believes in him shall not be confounded. Unless God professed himself the builder of an earthly work, so as not to signify of his own Christ, who was to be the foundation of believers in him, upon which, according as each shall have built up doctrine worthy or unworthy, if his work shall be proved by fire, if a reward shall be paid him by fire, it is the Creator's, because by fire your superstructure is judged — upon his own foundation, namely, that is, his own Christ. Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If man — both substance and work and image and likeness, both flesh through earth and soul through the breath of the Creator — then the whole God of Marcion dwells in another's property, if we are not the temple of the Creator. But if anyone shall defile the temple of God, he shall be defiled — surely by the God of the temple. By threatening an avenger you will be threatening the Creator. Be foolish, that you may be wise. Why? For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. With what God? If our former arguments have decided nothing for us toward this sense too, well that he here too builds up: For it is written, He that takes the wise in their craftiness; and again, The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. For it will in sum have been prescribed by us that the apostle could use no sentence of that God whom he ought to destroy, if he were not teaching him. Therefore, he says, let no one glory in man. And this according to the Creator's discipline: Wretched is the man who has hope in man! and, It is good to trust in God rather than to trust in men; and so, to glory likewise.

7. And the hidden things of darkness he himself will illuminate — surely through Christ, who promised Christ as illumination, who declared himself also a lamp, searching hearts and reins. From him too shall be praise to each one, from whom too the contrary of praise, as from a judge. Surely, you say, here at least he interprets world as the God of the world, by saying, We have been made a spectacle to the world and to angels and to men. For if by world he had meant the men of the world, he would not afterwards have named men also. Nay, lest you should argue thus, the providence of the Holy Spirit showed how he had said, We have been made a spectacle to the world — namely, to the angels who minister to the world, and to the men whom they serve. For the force of so great a constancy, not to say the Holy Spirit, feared — writing especially to sons whom he had begotten in the gospel — to name freely the God of the world, against whom he could not seem to preach except expressly. I do not defend, according to the law of the Creator, that he who had his father's wife was displeasing to him. He followed the discipline of the common and public religion. But when he condemns the same man to be delivered to Satan, he is the herald of a condemning God. Let it be seen too how he said, Unto the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord, since he judged both of the destruction of the flesh and of the salvation of the spirit, and, in bidding evil to be taken away from the midst, recalled a most frequent sentence of the Creator. Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Therefore the unleavened bread were figures of ourselves with the Creator. So too our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed. Why is Christ the Passover, if the Passover were not a figure of Christ, by the likeness of the saving blood and of the flock of Christ? Why does he clothe us and Christ with the images of the Creator's solemnities, if they were not ours? But, turning us from fornication, he makes manifest the resurrection of the flesh. The body, he says, is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body — as the temple for God, and God for the temple. The temple, then, for God shall perish, and God for the temple. But you see, He that raised up the Lord will raise us up also — and will raise us up in the body too, because the body is for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And well that he heaps up, Do you not know that your bodies are the members of Christ? What will the heretic say? Shall the members of Christ not rise again, which are now no longer ours? For we were bought with a great price. With none at all, surely, if Christ was a phantasm and had no substance of body which he might pay for our bodies. Therefore Christ both had wherewith to redeem us, and if with something great he redeemed these bodies — into which the same fornication shall not be committed, since they are now Christ's members and not ours — surely he will keep safe for himself what he purchased at a great price. How now shall we honour, how take up, God in a body that is to perish? Then follows his engaging upon marriage, which Marcion, more constant than the apostle, forbids. For the apostle, though he prefers the good of continence, yet permits marriage both to be contracted and to be in use, and advises rather to keep it than to put it asunder. Plainly Christ forbids divorce, but Moses permits it. Marcion, taking away all conjugal intercourse from the faithful (let his catechumens see to it), ordering repudiation before marriage — whose sentence does he follow, Moses' or Christ's? But Christ too, when he commands that a woman should not depart from her husband, or, if she has departed, should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, both permitted repudiation, which he did not wholly forbid, and confirmed marriage, which he first forbade to be put asunder, and, if perchance put asunder, willed to be reformed. But what causes does he give for continence too? Because the time is contracted. I had thought it because another God is in Christ; and yet, from him by whom is the contraction of time, will come also that which suits the contraction of time. No one takes thought for another's time. You affirm your God to be petty, Marcion, whom in anything the Creator's time straitens. Surely, when he prescribes that one must marry only in the Lord, lest a faithful man contract a heathen marriage, he upholds the law of the Creator, who everywhere forbids marriages with men of other tribes. But, Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in the heavens or on earth, it appears how he said it: not as though they truly were, but because there are those who are called so, when they are not. For he had begun, about to dispute of things offered to idols: We know that an idol is nothing. But the Creator even Marcion does not deny to be God; therefore the apostle cannot seem to have placed the Creator too among those who are called gods and yet are not — since, even if they were, yet to us there would be one God the Father. From whom are all things to us, except him whose are all things? Which things are these? You have in what precedes, All things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. So fully does he make the Creator the God of all, from whom are both the world and life and death, which cannot be of another God. From him, therefore, among all things, is Christ too. Teaching that each ought to live by his own labour, he had set before enough examples of soldiers, shepherds, husbandmen; but divine authority was wanting to him. He therefore opposes to the ungrateful the law of the Creator, which he was destroying; for of his own God he had no such law. You shall not muzzle, he says, the ox that treads out the corn; and he adds, Does it concern the Lord about oxen? — yes, even about oxen kind, for men's sake? For it is written for our sakes, he says. Therefore he both approved the allegorical law according to us, and as advocating for those who live of the gospel, and on this account that the evangelists are of no other than him whose is the law that looked forward to them, when he says, For it is written for our sakes. But he was unwilling to use the power of the law, because he preferred to labour for nothing. This he referred to his own glory, which he denied that anyone would make void — not to the destruction of the law, which he proved another would use. For behold, blind Marcion stumbles even upon the rock from which our fathers drank in the wilderness. For if that rock was Christ, surely it was the Creator's, whose also was the people. Of what is he interpreting a figure of a stranger sacrament? Or is it that he might teach this very thing, that the old things were figured unto a Christ to be reviewed out of them? For, about to run through the rest of the people's outcome too, he sends before, But these things were made examples to us. Tell me: were examples made to men by the Creator of another and unknown God, or does one God borrow examples from another — and that a rival? It frightens me about him from whom he transfers my faith to himself. Will the adversary make me better toward him? Now if I sin in the same things as the people, am I to suffer the same things, or not? But if not the same, in vain does he set before me to be feared what I am not to suffer. But from whom shall I suffer? If from the Creator, what is it his to inflict? And what manner of thing will it be that a zealous God should punish the sinner of his rival rather than, on the contrary, cherish him? If from that God of yours? But he knows not to punish. Thus this whole proposition of the apostle stands by no reason, if it is not the Creator's discipline. In short, even in the close he answers his preface. But these things, as they happened to them, were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. O Creator, both foreknowing now and admonishing the Christians of another! I pass over, when sometimes there are things equal to those already reviewed, certain of which I also briefly dismiss. A great argument of another God: the permission of all victuals against the law. As though we too did not confess that the burdens of the law were dismissed — but by him who imposed them, who promised renewal. So too he gave back the foods he took away, which he had furnished from the beginning. But if any other God had been the destroyer of our God, he would have forbidden his own nothing more than to live off the supplies of the adversary.

8. The head of the man is Christ. What Christ, who is not the author of man? For he set down head as authority, and authority will be of no other than the author. Of what man, then, is he the head? Surely of him concerning whom he subjoins, For a man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image of God. Therefore, if he is the image of the Creator (for the Creator, looking upon his Word, Christ, as the man to be, said, Let us make man after our image and likeness), how can I have another as my head, not him whose image I am? For since I am the image of the Creator, there is no room in me for another head. But also, why ought the woman to have power over her head? If it is because she is of the man and made for the man's sake, according to the institution of the Creator, then here too the apostle has taken care of his discipline, of whose institution he interprets the reasons of the discipline. He adds also, On account of the angels. What angels? that is, of whom? If apostates of the Creator, with reason — that, by that very countenance which gave them offence, she might carry a certain mark of the humility of her dress and the obscuring of her comeliness. But if on account of the angels of another God, what does he fear, if not even the Marcionites themselves desire women? We have often already shown that heresies are set among evils as an evil with the apostle, and that those are to be understood as approved who flee heresies as an evil. So likewise, in the sacrament of the bread and cup, we have already proved in the gospel the truth of the Lord's body and blood against the phantasm of Marcion. But also that every mention of judgement befits the Creator, as the God who judges, has been treated through almost the whole work. Now I speak of spiritual gifts, that these too were promised in Christ by the Creator, under that most just prescription, I think, by which the exhibition is to be believed of no other than him whose promise has been proved. Isaiah pronounced, A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from the root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him. Then he enumerates its kinds: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, and the Spirit of knowledge and of godliness; the Spirit of the fear of God shall fill him. For he showed that Christ should arise in the figure of a flower from a rod that issued from the root of Jesse — that is, the virgin of the lineage of David, the son of Jesse — in which Christ the whole substance of the Spirit was to consist, not as though to come upon him afterwards who was always the Spirit of God, even before the flesh — lest from this you argue that the prophecy pertains to that Christ who, as a mere man, only out of the reckoning of David, should afterwards obtain the Spirit of his God — but because from the time he flowered in the flesh, taken from the stock of David, all working of spiritual grace had to rest in him, and to leave off and make an end, as far as concerns the Jews; as the very fact testifies, that thenceforth nothing of the Creator's Spirit breathes among them, the wise and prudent architect and counsellor and prophet having been taken away from Judaea, so that this is the meaning of, The law and the prophets were until John. Now receive how, after Christ's reception into heaven, he pronounced that gifts of grace would come. He ascended on high, that is, into heaven; he led captivity captive, that is, death or human bondage; he gave gifts to the sons of men, that is, donatives, which we call charismata. Elegantly he says to the sons of men, not at random to men, showing us the sons of men, that is, of true men, namely of the apostles. For in the gospel, he says, I have begotten you; and, My sons, of whom I am again in travail. Now too that promise of the Spirit made absolutely through Joel: In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters shall prophesy, and upon my menservants and maidservants of my Spirit will I pour out. And surely, if in the last days the Creator promised the grace of the Spirit, and Christ the dispenser of spiritual things appeared in the last days — the apostle saying, But when the time was fulfilled, God sent his Son, and again, Because the time is now contracted — it appears, from the preaching of the last times too, that this grace of the Spirit pertains to the Christ of the Creator who preached it. Compare, then, the kinds in the apostle and in Isaiah. To one, he says, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom: at once Isaiah too set down the Spirit of wisdom. To another the word of knowledge: this will be the Spirit of understanding and counsel. To another faith in the same Spirit: this will be the Spirit of godliness and the fear of God. To another the gift of healings, to another of mighty works: this will be the Spirit of might. To another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues: this will be the Spirit of knowledge. See the apostle, both in making the distribution of the one Spirit and in interpreting its particularity, conspiring with the prophet. I can say that the very one who fitted the unity of the various charismata to the framework of our body through many and diverse members showed the same to be Lord both of the human body and of the Holy Spirit, who would not have the merit of the charismata be in the body of the spirit, which he placed not even in the human body; who too, concerning love which is to be set before all charismata, instructed the apostle by the chief precept, which Christ also approved: You shall love the Lord with your whole heart and with all your strength and with all your soul, and your neighbour as yourself. And though this was written in the law, he recalls that the Creator would speak in other tongues and in other lips; and with this commemoration he confirms the gift of tongues, nor can he here be seen to have confirmed a strange gift by the preaching of the Creator. Likewise, in prescribing silence to women in the church, that they should not speak even for the sake of learning (for the right of prophesying he has already shown that they too have, when he imposes a veil on a woman even when prophesying), he takes from the law the authority for the subjection of the woman — which, to say it once for all, he ought not to have known except for its destruction. But that we may now withdraw from spiritual matters, the very facts ought to prove which of us rashly claims his God, and whether these things can be opposed to our side; and whether, if the Creator promised in his own Christ not yet revealed — destined, namely, for the Jews only — operations to be had in their own time, in his own Christ, and among his own people. Let Marcion, therefore, exhibit the gifts of his God: some prophets, who yet have spoken not from human sense but from the Spirit of God, who have both foretold things to come and laid bare the secrets of the heart; let him put forth some psalm, some vision, some prayer, only let it be spiritual, in ecstasy, that is, in rapture, if any interpretation of a tongue has come in; let him prove to me too that some woman among him has prophesied, of those holier women of his that he boasts of: if all these things are more readily produced by me — and surely conspiring with the rules and arrangements and disciplines of the Creator — without doubt both the Christ and the Spirit and the apostle will be my God's. He has my profession, whoever shall wish to demand it. Meanwhile the Marcionite will exhibit nothing of this kind, who already fears to pronounce whose his Christ is, not yet revealed. Just as mine is to be awaited, who has been preached from the beginning, his on that account is not, because he is not from the beginning. Better that we believe in a Christ to come than the heretic in none. How some at that time denied the resurrection of the dead must first be looked into. Surely in the same way as now too; since the resurrection of the flesh is always denied. For the soul most even of the wise, claiming it divine, promise that it is saved; and the very common folk venerate their dead with that presumption by which they trust that their souls remain. But that bodies, whether by fires at once, or by wild beasts, or even most carefully preserved, are yet abolished in time, is manifest. If, therefore, the apostle rebuts those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, surely against them he upholds what they denied, namely the resurrection of the flesh. You have the answer in compendium; the rest now out of abundance. For the very thing that it is called the resurrection of the dead requires the properties of the words to be defended. Thus a thing is not dead except what has lost the soul by whose faculty it lived. The body is what loses the soul, and by losing it becomes dead; so the term dead befits the body. Further, if the resurrection is of the dead, and the dead is nothing else than the body, the resurrection will be of the body. So too the term resurrection claims no other thing than what fell. For rising can be said even of what did not fall at all, what always lay before. But to rise again is only of what fell; for, by rising again, because it fell, it is said to rise again. For the syllable RE is always applied to repetition. We say, then, that the body falls into the earth through death, as the very fact testifies, by the law of God. For to the body it was said, You are earth, and into earth you shall go. Thus what is of earth shall go into earth. This falls, which goes into earth; this rises again, which falls. Because through a man came death, through a man too the resurrection. Here too Christ's body is shown to me in the name of man, who consists of a body, as we have often already taught. But if in Christ we are all made alive even as we are killed in Adam — since in Adam we are killed in body, so of necessity in Christ we are made alive in body.
