For the rest, the likeness does not hold if the making-alive in Christ does not concur in the same substance of the killing in Adam. But he interposed something further about Christ, not to be omitted on account of the present dispute. For the resurrection of the flesh will be the more proved, the more I show Christ to be of that God with whom the resurrection of the flesh is believed. When he says, For he must reign till he puts his enemies under his feet, even from this already he proclaims an avenging God, and thereupon him who promised this to Christ: Sit at my right hand, till I make your enemies the footstool of your feet: the Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength out of Sion, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies. But it is necessary that I defend, as belonging to my sense, those scriptures which the Jews too try to take away from us. They say, then, that this psalm sang of Hezekiah, because he sat at the right hand of the temple, and God turned away and consumed his enemies; and that therefore the rest too, Before the morning-star from the womb I begot you, agrees with Hezekiah and with Hezekiah's birth. We bring forth the gospels (of whose credit we ought surely already in so great a work to have confirmed these men in something), declaring the Lord by a nocturnal nativity — so that this is, before the morning-star — and rather from the star understood, and from the testimony of the angel who by night announced to the shepherds that Christ was just then born, and from the place of the birth, for it is to an inn that men gather at night. Perhaps it was mystically done that Christ should be born by night, who was to be the light of truth in the darkness of ignorance. But neither would God have said, I begot you, except to a true son. For though of the whole people he says, I have begotten sons, yet he did not add, From the womb. But why did he add, From the womb, so vainly, as though it could be doubted of any man that he was born from the womb, unless because he wished it more curiously understood concerning Christ: From the womb I begot you, that is, from the womb alone, without the seed of man, ascribing to the flesh out of the womb what is of the spirit? This too befits him here: You are a priest for ever. But Hezekiah was neither a priest, nor for ever, even had he been one. After the order, he says, of Melchizedek. What has Hezekiah to do with Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High, and that uncircumcised, who blessed Abraham already circumcised after receiving the oblation of tithes? But the order of Melchizedek will agree with Christ, since indeed Christ is the proper and lawful high priest of God, the pontiff of an uncircumcised priesthood, then established among the nations, by whom he was rather to be received — about at some time to acknowledge both circumcision and the race of Abraham, when at last he comes, and will deem them worthy of acceptance and blessing. There is also another psalm beginning thus: God, give your judgement to the king — that is, to the Christ who is to reign — and your righteousness to the king's son — that is, to the people of Christ. For his sons are they who are reborn in him. But this psalm too will be said to sing of Solomon. Yet, since the things that befit Christ alone cannot teach that the rest too pertain not to Solomon but to Christ? He came down, he says, like rain upon the fleece, and like drops distilling upon the earth — describing his placid and imperceptible descent from heaven into flesh. But Solomon, even if he came down from somewhere, yet not like rain, because not from heaven. But I will propose simpler things. He shall have dominion, he says, from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. This is given to Christ alone; for the rest, Solomon ruled over the one and small Judaea. All kings shall adore him. Which all, except Christ? And all nations shall serve him. To which all, except Christ? Let his name be for ever. Whose name is for ever, except Christ's? Before the sun shall his name endure. For before the sun is the Word of God, that is, Christ. And in him shall all the peoples be blessed. In Solomon no nation is blessed, but in Christ every one. What now, if this psalm shows him to be God too? And they shall call him blessed; because, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders: blessed be the name of his glory, and the whole earth shall be filled with his glory. Against this, Solomon — I dare to say — lost even the glory he had in God, dragged through a woman even into idolatry. And so, since in the midst of the psalm this too is set, His enemies shall lick the dust, subjected, namely, to his feet, it will pertain to that on account of which I both brought in this psalm and defended it to my sense, that I might confirm both the glory of the kingdom and the subjection of the enemies according to the arrangement of the Creator, about to obtain it, to be believed of no other than the Creator's.

10. Let us return now to the resurrection, which we have indeed satisfied elsewhere too in a proper volume, resisting all heretics; but here too we are not wanting, on account of those who do not know that little work. What, he says, shall they do who are baptised for the dead, if the dead rise not? See to it, this institution. The Kalends of February, perchance, will answer to that of asking for the dead. Do not, then, straightway brand the apostle as a new author or confirmer of it, since it was the more to establish the resurrection of the flesh, in that those who were vainly baptised for the dead did this in faith of the resurrection. We have him somewhere as the definer of one baptism. Therefore to be baptised for the dead too is to be baptised for bodies; for we have shown the dead to be the body. What shall they do who are baptised for bodies, if bodies rise not? And so rightly do we fix this step, that the apostle introduced his second disputation likewise concerning the body. But some will say, How do the dead rise? and with what body do they come? For the resurrection being defended, which was denied, it was consequent to treat of the quality of the body, which was not seen. But of that it is fitting to engage with others. For Marcion, in no wise admitting the resurrection of the flesh, and promising salvation to the soul alone, makes a question not of quality but of substance. But even from these things he is most manifestly hedged in, which the apostle treats concerning the quality of the body, on account of those who say, How shall the dead rise? and with what body do they come? For he has now preached that the body shall rise, if he treated of the body's quality. In short, if he proposes examples of a grain of wheat or of any such thing, or to which God shall give a body as he will; if he says that to each of the seeds there is its own body, so that there is one flesh of men, another of cattle and birds, and bodies celestial and terrestrial, and one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars — does he not hold out a carnal and corporeal resurrection, which he commends by carnal and corporeal examples? does he not also pledge it from that God whose are the examples too? So too the resurrection, he says. How? Just as the grain is sown a body, it rises a body. He called the sowing, then, the dissolution of the body into the earth, because it is sown in corruption, in dishonour, in weakness. That same order which is in the dissolution is here too in the resurrection of the body, namely, as in the grain. For the rest, if you take away from the resurrection the body which you gave to the dissolution, where will the difference of the outcome stand? Likewise too, if it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body. And if the soul or the spirit has some proper body, so that the animal body can be seen to signify the soul, and the spiritual body the spirit, not on that account does he say that the soul shall be spirit in the resurrection, but the body, which, born with the soul and living through the soul, takes the name of animal, shall be spiritual, while it rises through the spirit into eternity. In short, if not the soul but the flesh is sown in corruption, while it is dissolved into the earth, then no longer will the soul be the animal body, but the flesh which was the animal body, since out of the animal is made the spiritual, as he also says below, Not first that which is spiritual. For to this end he forestructures even concerning Christ himself: The first man Adam was made into a living soul, the last Adam into a quickening spirit; though the most foolish heretic would not have it so, for he set down Lord instead of last Adam, fearing, namely, lest, if he had Lord as the last Adam, we should defend Christ also of the same one in the last Adam whose he is in the first. But the falsehood shines out. For why first Adam, except because there is also a last Adam? They have no order between them except things equal and of the same name or substance or author. For though there can in diverse things too be one first, another last, yet of one author. For the rest, if the author too is another, even he himself can indeed be called last. Yet what he introduced is first; but last only if it be equal to the first. But it is not equal to the first, because it is not of the same author. In the same way too he is convicted in the name of man. The first man, he says, of the dust earthy, the second Lord from heaven. Why second, if not a man, which the first too is? Or is the first too Lord, if the second is? But it is enough if in the gospel he applies to Christ Son of man and man, and in man Adam he cannot deny him. The sequel too presses him. For when the apostle says, As is the earthy — man, namely — such are the earthy also — men, surely — then also, As is the heavenly — man — such are the heavenly also — men. For he could not but have set heavenly men over against earthy men, that he might the more studiously distinguish their state and hope in the fellowship of the appellation. For he calls them earthy and heavenly men in state and hope, yet on a par, who according to their outcome are reckoned either in Adam or in Christ. And therefore now, to the exhortation of heavenly hope, As we have borne, he says, the image of the earthy, let us bear also the image of the heavenly — referring it not to any substance of the resurrection, but to the discipline of the present time. For, Let us bear, he says, not, We shall bear — preceptively, not promissively — wishing that we, just as he himself walked, so should walk, and depart from the image of the earthy, that is, the old man, which is the carnal working. In short, what does he subjoin? For this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God — the works, namely, of flesh and blood, by which too, writing to the Galatians, he took away the kingdom of God; being wont elsewhere too to put the substance for the works of the substance, as when he says that those who are in the flesh cannot please God. For when shall we be able to please God, except while we are in this flesh? Of working there is, I think, no other time. But if, though placed in the flesh, we flee the works of the flesh, then we shall not be in the flesh, while we are not in the substance of the flesh, but in the fault of it. But if under the name of flesh we are bidden to lay aside the works, not the substance, of the flesh, then to the works of the flesh, not to the substance of the flesh, under the name of flesh, is the kingdom of God denied. For that is not condemned in which evil is done, but that which is done. To give poison is a crime, yet the cup in which it is given is not guilty. So too the body is the vessel of carnal works, but the soul is what, being in it, tempers the poison of some evil deed. But what manner of thing is it that, if the soul, the authoress of the works of the flesh, shall earn the kingdom of God through the expiation of those things which it committed in the body, the body — a mere minister — should remain in damnation? Shall the cup be punished, the poisoner being absolved? And yet we do not at all defend the kingdom of God for the flesh, but the resurrection of its own substance, as the door of the kingdom, by which entrance is made. For the rest, the resurrection is one thing, the kingdom another. For first the resurrection, then the kingdom. We say, then, that the flesh rises, but, changed, obtains the kingdom. For the dead shall rise incorrupt — those, namely, who had been corrupt, their bodies fallen into dissolution. And we shall be changed, in a moment, in the momentary motion of an eye. For this corruptible — holding, surely, his own flesh, the apostle was saying — must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality, that the substance, namely, may be made fit for the kingdom of God. For we shall be as the angels. This will be the transformation of the flesh, but of the flesh raised up. Or if there shall be none, how shall it put on incorruption and immortality? Made another, then, through transformation, it shall then obtain the kingdom of God — no longer flesh nor blood, but what God shall have given to it for a body. And therefore rightly the apostle: Flesh and blood shall not obtain the kingdom of God — ascribing it to the transformation which comes after the resurrection. But if then shall come to pass the word that is written with the Creator, Where, death, is your victory or your contention? Where, death, is your sting? (and this word is the Creator's through the prophet), his too will be the thing — that is, the kingdom — whose word shall come to pass in the kingdom. Nor does he give thanks to another God, in that he received for us, surely, victory over death and triumph.

11. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. If the word God has become common through the fault of human error, in that many are called and believed gods in the world, yet the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ will be understood as no other than the Creator, who both blessed the universe (you have Genesis) and is blessed by the universe (you have Daniel). Likewise, if a father can be called the father of no God more than of the Creator, yet the Father of mercies will be the same who has been called merciful and compassionate and most rich in mercy. You have in Jonah the very example of mercy, which he furnished to the Ninevites entreating him; easy to be bent too by Hezekiah's weeping, and by Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, beseeching that the blood of Naboth be forgiven, and by David acknowledging his sin to indulge at once — preferring, namely, the repentance of the sinner to his death, out of the affection of mercy. If the God of Marcion has produced or pronounced anything of the kind, I will acknowledge the Father of mercies. But if from the time he was revealed he ascribes this title to him, as though from then he were the Father of mercies, from when he set about to free mankind — but we too from that time deny him, from which he is said to be revealed. He cannot, then, ascribe anything to him whom he then shows when he ascribes anything to him. For if he were first established to be, then something could be ascribed to him too. For what is ascribed is an accident, but accidents are preceded by the showing of the very thing to which they happen — especially when what is ascribed to him who has not first been shown is already another's. He will the more be denied to be, the more that by which he is affirmed to be is of him who has already been shown. So too the new testament will be of no other than him who promised it; and if not the letter, yet his spirit; this will be the newness. In short, he who had cut the letter on tablets of stone, the same had also pronounced concerning the spirit, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. And if the letter kills, but the spirit makes alive, both are his who says, I will kill and I will make alive, I will smite and I will heal. We have of old claimed the twofold power of the Creator, both of judge and of good: of the letter killing through the law, and of the spirit making alive through the gospel. Things which, though diverse, were first reviewed with one — these cannot make two gods. He commemorates too of the veil of Moses, by which he covered his face, incontemplable to the sons of Israel. If for this reason, that he might defend the greater splendour of the new testament, which abides in glory, than of the old, which had to be made void, this too suits my faith, which prefers the gospel to the law; and see whether it suits mine the more. For there will be a setting of something over a thing where there was also that over which it is set. But when he says, But the senses of the world were blunted — surely not of the Creator, but of the people, who is in the world. For of Israel he says, To this day that same veil is upon their heart. He shows that the veil of the face in Moses was a figure of the veil of the heart in the people, because not even now is Moses perceived among them by the heart, just as not then by the face. What is it, then, that is still veiled in Moses which pertains to Paul, if the Creator's Christ preached by Moses has not yet come? how are the hearts of the Jews still noted as covered and veiled, the preachings of Moses concerning Christ — in whom they ought to understand him — not yet exhibited? What has it to do with an apostle of another Christ, that the Jews did not understand the sacraments of their own God — except because the veil of their heart pertained to the blindness by which they had not perceived the Christ of Moses? In short, what follows, But when it shall be turned to God, the veil shall be taken away, this he says properly of the Jew, with whom is the veil of Moses, who, when he shall have passed into the faith of Christ, understands that Moses preached of Christ. But how shall the veil of the Creator be taken away in the Christ of another God, whose sacraments the Creator could not have veiled — unknown things, namely, of one unknown? He says, then, that we now, with open face — namely of the heart, which is veiled in the Jews — beholding Christ, are transfigured into the same image from glory, by which, namely, Moses too was transfigured from the glory of the Lord, into glory. Thus, setting forth the bodily illumination of Moses from his meeting with the Lord, and the bodily veil from the weakness of the people, and superinducing the spiritual revelation and spiritual splendour in Christ — as from the Lord, he says, of the spirits — he testifies that the whole order of Moses was a figure of a Christ ignored among the Jews, but acknowledged among us. We know that certain senses can suffer ambiguity from the sound of the pronunciation or the mode of the punctuation, when a doubleness of these intervenes. This Marcion seized, reading thus: In whom the God of this age — so as, by showing the Creator the God of this age, to suggest another God of another age. We, on the contrary, say it must be punctuated thus: In whom God, then: has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age; In whom, that is, in the unbelieving Jews, in whom the gospel was covered to some still under the veil of Moses. For God had threatened them — loving him with their lips, but in heart standing far off from him: With the ear you shall hear and not hear, with the eyes you shall see and not see; and, Unless you believe, neither shall you understand; and, I will take away the wisdom of the wise and make void the prudence of the prudent. But these things he was not threatening about hiding the gospel of an unknown God. So, even if he is the God of this age, yet of the unbelievers of this age he blinds the heart, because they did not of their own accord recognise his Christ, to be understood from the scriptures. And having treated thus far what is set in the ambiguity of punctuation, lest it profit the adversary — content with my victory, I can even pass over this whole contention altogether. For a simpler answer will be at hand: to interpret the lord of this age as the devil, who said, as the prophet reports, I will be like the Most High, I will set my throne in the clouds — as indeed the whole superstition of this age is enslaved to him who blinds the hearts of the unbelievers, and chiefly of the apostate Marcion. In short, he did not see the close of the sense meeting him: For God, who said out of darkness let light shine, has shone in our hearts, unto the illumination of the knowledge of himself in the person of Christ. Who said, Let there be light? And of the illumination of the world, who said to Christ, I have set you for a light of the nations — of those sitting, namely, in darkness and in the shadow of death? To whom the Spirit answers in the psalm, out of foresight of the future. The light of your countenance, he says, is signed upon us, Lord. But the countenance of God is Christ the Lord. Whence also the apostle above, Who is, he says, the image of God. Therefore, if Christ is the person of the Creator who says, Let there be light, then both Christ and the apostles and the gospel and the veil and Moses and the whole series, according to the testimony of the close, are of the Creator, the God of this age — certainly not of him who never said, Let there be light. I pass over here too about another epistle, which we have inscribed To the Ephesians, but the heretics To the Laodiceans. For he says that the nations should remember that at that time, when they were without Christ, aliens from Israel, without converse and testaments and the hope of promise, they were even without God — surely in the world, even if of the Creator. Therefore, if he said the nations were without God, but their God is the devil, not the Creator, it appears that by the lord of this age must be understood him whom the nations received in place of God, not the Creator, whom they do not know. But what manner of thing is it that the treasure should not be held to be of the same one whose are also the vessels in which it is — in our earthen vessels? For if it is the glory of God that so great a treasure should be held in earthen vessels, and the earthen vessels are the Creator's, then both the glory is the Creator's, whose vessels savour of the eminence of the power of God, and the very power; because for this reason it was committed into earthen vessels, that its eminence might be proved. For the rest, it will no longer be the glory of another God, and therefore not even his power, but rather a disgrace and weakness, whose eminence earthen and indeed alien vessels have received. But if these are the earthen vessels in which he says we suffer so much, in which too we carry about the mortification of God, the God is ungrateful and unjust enough, if he is not also to raise up this substance in which, for his faith, so much is endured, in which too the death of Christ is carried about, in which too the eminence of power is consecrated. For he proposes, That the life of Christ too may be made manifest in our body — namely, as his death too is carried about in the body. Of what life of Christ, then, does he speak? that by which we now live in him? And how in the sequel does he exhort, not to things visible nor temporal, but to things invisible and eternal — that is, not to things present, but to things future? But if he speaks of the future life of Christ, saying that it will appear in the body, he plainly preached the resurrection of the flesh — saying indeed that our outward man is corrupted, and not as though by eternal destruction after death, but by labours and discomforts, of which he sent before, adding, And we shall not fail. For in saying too that our inward man is renewed from day to day, here he shows both: both the corruption of the body from the vexation of temptations, and the renewal of the mind from the contemplation of the promises.

12. Of our earthly dwelling-place he does not say that we have a house eternal, not made with hands, in heaven, because what is made with hands of the Creator perishes wholly, dissolved after death. For, treating of these things to console the fear of death and the sadness of dissolution itself, he makes it more manifest too through the sequel, when he subjoins that we groan over this tabernacle of the earthly body, desiring to be clothed upon with that which is from heaven; since even, when despoiled, we shall not be found naked — that is, we shall receive what we were despoiled of, that is, the body. And again: For we who are in this tabernacle of the body groan, in that we are burdened, not wishing to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon. For here he expressed what in the first epistle he touched: And the dead shall rise incorrupt — those who have already died — and we shall be changed — we who shall be found by God in the flesh. For those too shall rise incorrupt, the body, namely, being recovered, and that entire, so that from this they may be incorrupt; and these, on account of the now last moment of time, and on account of the merits of the vexations of antichrist, by an abridgement of death, but changed, shall obtain rather to be clothed upon by that which is from heaven than to put off the body. So, if these put on over their body that heavenly thing, then surely the dead too shall receive a body over which they too may put on incorruption from heaven; because of them too he says, This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality. They put on, when they shall have received a body; these put on over, because they have not lost the body; and therefore not rashly did he say, not wishing to be unclothed of the body, but to be clothed upon — that is, not wishing to experience death, but to be anticipated by life, that this mortal may be swallowed up by life, while it is snatched from death through the over-garment of transformation. Therefore, because he shows this to be better, that we be not saddened by the anticipation of death, if it perchance come, he says too that we have from God an earnest of the Spirit, as though pledged unto the same hope of the over-garment; and that we are absent from the Lord so long as we are in the flesh, and on this account ought to count it good to be rather absent from the body and present with the Lord, that we may even gladly accept death. And so he says that we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive the things he did through the body, whether good or evil. For if then is the retribution of merits, how can some already be reckoned with God? And by naming a tribunal, and the reckoning of good and evil work, he shows the judge of either sentence, and confirmed the representation of all bodies. For what was committed in the body cannot but be judged in the body. For God is unjust, if a man is not punished or aided through that by which he wrought. If, then, there is any new condition in Christ, the old things have passed, behold all things are made new — the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled. If too he bids us cleanse ourselves from the defilement of flesh and blood, the substance does not receive the kingdom of God; if he destines too the church a holy virgin to be assigned to Christ — surely as a bride to a bridegroom — the image cannot be joined to one hostile to the truth of the thing itself. If he calls the false apostles deceitful workers, transfigurers of themselves, by hypocrisy, namely, of conduct, not of adulterated preaching, he taxes them. So fully was the difference about discipline, not about divinity. If Satan is transfigured into an angel of light, this cannot be directed against the Creator. For the Creator is God, not an angel; he would have been said to transfigure himself into a God of light, not into an angel, had he not signified that Satan whom both we and Marcion know to be an angel. Of paradise his pen is its own to every question it suffers. Here perhaps I shall wonder, if God could have a paradise of his own who has no terrestrial arrangement — unless he used the Creator's paradise too on sufferance, as he did the world. And yet to take up a man into heaven is the Creator's example, in Elijah. But I shall rather wonder that the Lord supremely good — to whom smiting and raging are alien — should have applied to his apostle, to buffet him, an angel of Satan, not even his own at least, but the Creator's, and, when besought thrice, should not have granted it. The God of Marcion, then, also corrects, emulating the Creator who casts down the proud — putting down, namely, the mighty from their throne. Or is he himself perchance the one who also gave Satan power over the body of Job, that virtue might be approved in weakness? Why too does the chastiser of the Galatians still hold the form of the law, prefixing that every word should stand by three witnesses? Why does he threaten that he will not spare sinners, the preacher of a most gentle God? Nay, he affirms that the very power of acting more harshly in their presence was given him by the Lord. Deny now, heretic, that your God is to be feared, whose apostle was feared!

13. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. When the work is being driven to a close, the things which recur must now be reviewed briefly, but some passed over which have recurred more often. It irks me to engage still about the law, who have so often proved that its concession furnishes no argument of a different God in Christ — being, namely, both preached and promised unto Christ with the Creator — inasmuch as this epistle too seems for the most part to exclude the law. But that God too is carried about by the apostle as judge we have often already shown, and in the judge an avenger, and the Creator in the avenger. So here too, when he says, For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone that believes, to Jew and Greek, because the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith — without doubt he reckons both gospel and salvation to a just God, not to a good one, so to speak, according to the heretic's distinction — transferring from the faith of the law to the faith of the gospel, of his own law surely and his own gospel. Since too he says that wrath is revealed from heaven upon the impiety and injustice of men, who hold the truth in injustice. Of what God's wrath? Surely the Creator's. Therefore his truth too will be whose is also the wrath, which is to be revealed in vengeance for the truth. Adding too, But we know that the judgement of God is according to truth, he both proved the wrath itself, from which comes judgement for truth, and again confirmed the truth of the same God whose wrath he proved by proving the judgement. It is another matter, if the Creator, angry, avenges the truth of another God held in injustice. But how great pits Marcion has made in this epistle especially, by taking away what he would, will appear from the integrity of our instrument. It is enough for me to take as negligences and blindnesses of his those things which he likewise did not see to be erased. For if God shall judge the secrets of men, both of those who sinned in the law and of those without law — because these too do not know the law, and by nature do the things of the law — surely that God shall judge whose are both the law and nature itself, which is, as it were, a law to those ignorant of the law. But how shall he judge? According to the gospel, he says, through Christ. Therefore both the gospel and Christ are his whose are also the law and nature, which shall be vindicated through the gospel and Christ — by that judgement of God, surely, which above too was according to truth. Therefore, since the wrath which is to be revealed from heaven for the defence of that truth is of none but the God of wrath, so too here this sense, cohering with the former, in which the judgement of the Creator is proclaimed, cannot be referred to another God, who neither judges nor is angry, but to him whose, while these are — I mean the judgement and the wrath — these too of necessity are: the gospel and Christ, through whom these have to be transacted. And therefore he inveighs against transgressors of the law — teaching not to steal, and stealing — as a man of the law of God, not as touching the Creator himself in these ways, who, even while forbidding to steal, commanded a fraud upon the Egyptians of gold and silver — just as they twist the rest too against him. Forsooth the apostle feared to make plain a reproach to the God from whom he did not fear to have departed! And so much had he assailed the Jews, that he heaped up the prophetic rebuke: On your account the name of God is blasphemed. How perverse, then, that he himself should blaspheme him for whose sake of being blasphemed he upbraids the wicked! He prefers too the circumcision of the heart to uncircumcision; with the God of the law was made the circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh, in spirit, not in letter. But if this is the circumcision of Jeremiah, And circumcise the foreskins of your heart, as Moses too said, Circumcise your hardness of heart — then his will be the spirit circumcising the heart whose is also the letter reaping its flesh, and his the Jew who is in secret whose too is the Jew in the open, because the apostle would not even name a Jew who was not the servant of the God of the Jews. Then the law, now the righteousness of God through the faith of Christ. What is this distinction? Did your God serve the arrangement of the Creator, giving him his time and his law? or is his now whose it then was? His is the law whose too is the faith of Christ; it is a distinction of arrangements, not of gods. He admonishes those justified by the faith of Christ, not by the law, to have peace toward God. Toward what God? Of whom we were nowhere enemies, or against whose law and nature we rebelled? For if peace is fitting with him with whom there was war, by him too we shall be justified, and his will be Christ, by whose faith we shall be justified, to whose peace it is fitting that his enemies should at some time be reduced. But the law, he says, entered in, that sin might abound. Why? That grace might superabound, he says. Of what God the grace, if not whose too is the law? Unless the Creator on this account intercalated the law, to procure the business of the grace of another God — and that a rival, not to say an unknown one — that, as with him sin had reigned unto death, so too grace might reign in righteousness unto life through Jesus Christ, his adversary. For this the law of the Creator had concluded all under sin, and had brought the whole world into guilt, and stopped every mouth, that none should glory through it, so that grace might be reserved unto the glory of Christ — not the Creator's, but Marcion's. I can here too forestructure concerning the substance of Christ, from the prospect of the following question. For he says, We are dead to the law. Therefore the body of Christ can even be contended to be a body, not at once flesh. But also, of whatever substance it be, when he names the body of him whom he subjoins to have risen from the dead, no other body can be understood than of flesh, against which the law of death was pronounced. But behold he both bears witness to the law and excuses it from the cause of sin. What then shall we say? Is the law sin? God forbid. Blush, Marcion. God forbid. The apostle abominates the accusation of the law. But I do not know sin except through the law. O highest proclamation hence of the law, through which it was made plain that sin lay hidden! Not, then, did the law seduce, but sin through the occasion of the precept. Why do you impute to the God of the law what the apostle does not dare to impute to his law? Nay, he heaps up: The law is holy, and its precept just and good. If he so venerates the law of the Creator, how he destroys the Creator himself I do not know. Who distinguishes two gods, one just, another good, when he ought to be believed both whose precept is both good and just? But if he also confirms the law to be spiritual, surely it is prophetic too, surely figurative too. For I ought even from this to constitute Christ figuratively preached in the law, in such a way that he could not be acknowledged by all the Jews.

14. If the Father sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, not on that account shall the flesh which appeared in him be called a phantasm. For he ascribed sin above to the flesh, and made it the law of sin dwelling in his members and warring against the law of the mind. For this reason, then, the Son was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, that he might redeem the flesh of sin by a like substance — that is, a fleshly one, which was like to the sinning flesh, while not itself sinning. For this too will be the power of God: in a like substance to perfect salvation. For it is no great thing if the Spirit of God should heal the flesh; but if flesh like to the sinning flesh, while it is flesh, but not of sin. Thus the likeness will pertain to the title of sin, not to a falsehood of substance. For he would not have added Of sin, if he wished a likeness of substance to be understood, so as to deny the truth; for he would have set down only Of flesh, not also Of sin. But when he so framed it, Of sinful flesh, he both confirmed the substance, that is, flesh, and referred the likeness to the vice of the substance, that is, to sin. Suppose now the likeness were said of substance — not on that account will the truth of substance be denied. Why, then, true, though like? Because true indeed, but not from seed, of a like state, but true of a reckoning not like, yet not unlike. For the rest, there is no likeness in contraries. Spirit would not be called the likeness of flesh, because flesh too would not take on a likeness of spirit; but it would be called a phantasm, if what was not appeared. But it is called a likeness when there is what appears. For it is, while it is the equal of another. But a phantasm, in that it only seems, is not a likeness. And here too, expounding how he would not have us be in the flesh, though we are in the flesh — that is, that we should not be in the works of the flesh — he shows that on this reasoning he wrote, Flesh and blood cannot obtain the kingdom of God: not condemning the substance, but its works; which, because they can not be admitted by us, though still placed in the flesh, will pertain not to the guilt of the substance, but of the conduct. Likewise, if the body indeed is dead because of sin — so that it is the death not of the soul but of the body — but the spirit is life because of righteousness, to which death came because of sin, that is, to the body. For nothing is restored except to him who lost it; and so there will be a resurrection of the dead, since it is of bodies. For he subjoins: He who raised Christ from the dead shall make alive your mortal bodies too. So fully did he both confirm the resurrection of the flesh — without which neither can a thing be called body nor anything else understood as mortal — and prove the bodily substance of Christ; since our mortal bodies too shall likewise be made alive, just as he too was raised up — not otherwise, namely, than because in the body. Here too I leap over a most ample chasm of intercepted scripture, but I lay hold of the apostle bearing witness to Israel that they have a zeal of God — their own, surely — yet not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God, he says, and seeking to set up their own righteousness, that is, of their own law, they did not submit themselves to the righteousness of God; for Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness to everyone that believes. Here will be the heretic's argument: that the Jews were ignorant of the superior God, against whom they set up their own righteousness, that is, of their own law, not receiving Christ, the end of the law. Why then does he bear witness of their zeal toward their own God, if he does not also upbraid them with ignorance toward the same God? — that they were indeed driven by zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, being ignorant of him, namely, while they are ignorant of his arrangements in Christ, the consummation that was to stand for the law, and so maintain their own righteousness against him. And so the Creator himself too attests their ignorance toward himself: Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood me; and that they would rather set up their own righteousness, teaching doctrines the precepts of men, and were also gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ — out of ignorance, namely. Nothing, therefore, can be expounded as of another God which befits the Creator, because otherwise the apostle would undeservedly have branded the Jews with ignorance toward an unknown God. For wherein had they sinned, if they set up the righteousness of their own God against him whom they were ignorant of? But behold he exclaims: O the depth of the riches and wisdom of God, and his ways past tracing out! Whence that outburst? Out of the remembrance, namely, of the scriptures which he had unrolled before, out of the contemplation of the sacraments which he had above expounded, of the faith of Christ coming out of the law. If Marcion erased these of set purpose, why does his apostle exclaim, beholding no riches of a God so poor and beggarly as one who founded nothing, preached nothing, lastly possessed nothing, as one who descends into another's property? But the wealth and riches of the Creator, once hidden, are now unlocked. For so he had promised: And I will give them hidden treasures, I will open the invisible to them. Thence, then, it was exclaimed: O the depth of the riches and wisdom of God! whose treasures now lay open. This is Isaiah's, and the sequel too is from the instrument of the same prophet: For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who was his counsellor? who has first given to him, and it shall be recompensed to him? You who took away so much from the scriptures, why did you keep these things, as though they too were not the Creator's? Plainly, let us see the precepts of the new God. Hating, he says, evil, and cleaving to good. Is it another thing with the Creator, Take away evil from you, and Turn away from evil and do good? Affectioned to one another in brotherly love; for it is not the very same as, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Rejoicing in hope — of God, surely. For it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in magistrates. Enduring tribulation. For the Lord shall hear you in the day of tribulation. You have the psalm. Bless, and curse not. Who shall teach this but he who founded all things with blessings? Not minded on high things, but consenting to the lowly; be not wise in your own eyes. For they hear Woe through Isaiah. Render to no one evil for evil. And, Remember not the malice of your brother. Nor avenging yourselves. For vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord. Have peace with all men. Therefore the legal retaliation too did not permit the recompensing of injury, but checked its inception through fear of recompense. With reason, then, he concluded the whole discipline of the Creator in his chief precept, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. If this supplement of the law is from the law itself, what God is the God of the law I now do not know. I fear it is the God of Marcion. But if the gospel of Christ is fulfilled by this precept, and it is Christ's, not the Creator's, by which now we contend — did Christ say or not, I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil it? In vain did Pontus labour to deny that sentence. If the gospel did not fulfil the law, behold the law fulfilled the gospel. But well that in the close too he threatens the tribunal of Christ — surely of the judge and avenger, surely of the Creator — establishing him certainly as one to be propitiated whom he holds out as to be feared, even if he were preaching another.

15. ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. It will not weary me to attend to the shorter epistles too. There is savour even in few things. The Jews had killed their own prophets. I can say, What has this to do with an apostle of another and indeed a supremely good God, who is said not even to condemn the offences of his own, and who too, by destroying those same prophets, in a manner slays them himself? For what evil did Israel commit with him, if it killed those whom he too reprobated, if he first pronounced a hostile sentence against them? But it sinned with their own God. He upbraided the iniquity to whom the injured one belongs; surely it is anyone rather than the adversary of the injured. But neither would he have loaded them by imputing the slaying of the Lord too, who both killed the Lord, by saying, and their own prophets — though Their own is the heretic's addition. For what so bitter, if they slew Christ the preacher of another God, who butchered the prophets of their own God? But the standing of the heightening is, that they had slain both the Lord and his servants. In short, if they slew the Christ of one God, the prophets of another, he equalled the impieties, he did not heighten them. But they were not to be equalled; therefore they could not be heightened, except the offences out of either title were committed against the same Lord. Therefore of the same God are both the Christ and the prophets. But what holiness he calls the will of God you would recognise from the contraries which he forbids. For he says, To abstain from fornication, not from marriage; that each should know how to treat his own vessel in honour. How? while not in lust, as the nations. But lust is not, even among the nations, ascribed to marriage, but to extraordinary and unnatural and monstrous things. The law of nature is contrary to luxury, and to baseness too and uncleanness, which excludes not marriage but lust, which would treat our vessel in the honour of marriage. But this passage I have treated with the precedence reserved for the other — that is, the fuller — holiness, preferring continence and virginity to marriage, but not to forbidden marriages. For I rebut the destroyers of the God of marriage, not the followers of chastity. He says that those who remain unto the coming of Christ, together with those who are dead in Christ, who shall first rise, shall be caught up in the clouds into the air, to meet the Lord. I recognise the heavenly substances themselves — even Jerusalem which is above — marvelling at these things already then foreseen, and announcing through Isaiah, Who are these that fly hither like clouds, and like doves with their young to me? If Christ has prepared this ascent for us, that will be the Christ of whom Amos says: Who builds his ascent into the heavens — surely for himself and his own. Thereafter from whom shall I now hope, except from him from whom I heard these things? Whose Spirit does he forbid to be quenched, and what prophecies does he forbid to be held as nothing? Surely not the Creator's Spirit, nor the Creator's prophecies, according to Marcion. For what he destroys, he has already quenched and made nothing, nor can he forbid that which he made nothing. Therefore it lies upon Marcion to exhibit today in his church the Spirit of his God, thenceforth, which is not to be quenched, and prophecies which are not to be held as nothing. And if he has exhibited what he thinks, let him know that we shall challenge whatever it be to the form of spiritual and prophetic grace and power, that it should both foretell things to come and reveal the secrets of the heart and expound mysteries. When he shall have produced and proved nothing of the kind, we shall produce both the Spirit and the prophecies of the Creator, foretelling according to himself. And so it will be established of whom the apostle spoke — namely, of those things which were to be in the church of that God who, while he is, his Spirit too works, and his promise is celebrated. Come now, you who deny the salvation of the flesh, and, whenever the body is named in such a context, interpret it as some other thing I know not what than the substance of the flesh — how did the apostle distinguish all in their new substances by definite names, and set all in the one matter of salvation, wishing that our spirit and body and soul be preserved without complaint at the coming of our Saviour Christ? For he set down both soul and body, as two things, so as two distinct ones. For though the soul too has a body of its own quality, as the spirit also, yet since both body and soul are distinctly named, the soul has its own proper term, not needing the common term of body; that is left to the flesh, which, not named by its own, must of necessity use the common one. For I see no other substance in man, after spirit and soul, to which the term body may be accommodated, except the flesh — understanding this so often under the name of body, as often as it is not named; much more here, since what is called body is named by its own name.

16. ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. We are compelled to repeat certain things again and again, that we may confirm by them what coheres. We say that here too the Lord, the recompenser of either merit, is carried about by the apostle — either the Creator, or, what Marcion would not have, the equal of the Creator — with whom it is just that to our afflicters affliction should be repaid, and to us, who are afflicted, rest, in the revelation of the Lord Jesus coming from heaven with the angels of his power and in a flame of fire. But the flame and fire which I defend the heretic has quenched, lest, namely, he should make the God ours. Yet the vanity of the erasure shines out. For when the apostle writes that the Lord will come to vengeance, to be exacted of those who know not God and who obey not the gospel — whom he says shall pay a penalty of destruction, eternal, from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might — it follows that he introduces a flame of fire, namely, coming to punish. So here too, though Marcion be unwilling, Christ is of the burning God, and in that other it is the Creator's, that he avenges himself even on those who know not the Lord, that is, on the heathen. For he set apart, Those who obey not the gospel — whether Christian sinners or Jews. Further, to exact penalties of the heathen, who perchance do not know the gospel, is not the part of that God who is naturally unknown, and is nowhere revealed except in the gospel, not knowable to all. But to the Creator even a natural acknowledgement is owed, by understanding from his works and thence seeking unto fuller knowledge. His, therefore, it is to strike even those ignorant of God, whom it is not lawful to be ignorant of. The very thing he says, From the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might, using the words of Isaiah, savours from the very cause of the same Lord rising up to shatter the earth. But who is the man of sin, the son of perdition, who must first be revealed before the Lord's coming, exalting himself above all that is called God and above all religion, about to sit in the temple of God and to boast himself God? According to us, indeed, antichrist, as the old and new prophecies teach, as John the apostle, who says that already the antichrists have gone forth into the world, forerunners of the spirit of antichrist, denying that Christ has come in the flesh, and dissolving Jesus — namely, in God the Creator: but according to Marcion, I do not know whether he be the Christ of the Creator. He has not yet come, with him. But whichever of the two he is, I ask why he comes in all power and signs and lying wonders? Therefore, he says, because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved; and for this there shall be sent them a working of deceit, that all may be judged who believed not the truth, but consented to iniquity. Therefore, if it is antichrist — and according to the Creator — then the Creator will be God who sends him to thrust into error those who believed not the truth that they might be saved; his too will be the truth and salvation who avenges them by the suggestion of error — that is, the Creator's, to whom the very zeal belongs of deceiving by error those whom he did not take by truth. But if it is not antichrist, according to us, then it is the Christ of the Creator, according to Marcion. And what manner of thing will it be that, to avenge his own truth, he should send the Christ of the Creator? But if he agrees too about antichrist, I shall likewise say: What manner of thing is it that Satan, an angel of the Creator, should be necessary to him, and be slain by him, having to discharge the working of deceit for the Creator? In sum, if it is beyond doubt that the angel and the truth and the salvation are his whose are also the wrath and the emulation and the sending of deceits against the despisers and deserters, even against the ignorant (so that now Marcion too may come down a step, conceding his God too to be a zealous one) — who shall more worthily be angry? I think, he who from the beginning of things prepared nature by works, benefits, plagues, preachings, witnesses, unto the acknowledgement of himself, and yet was not acknowledged; or he who once, by the single instrument of the gospel — and that uncertain, surely not openly preaching another God — was brought forth? So, to whom vengeance befits, to him will befit the material of vengeance — I mean the gospel, and the truth and salvation. But that he should bid him work who would eat, is the discipline of him who ordered a free mouth for the ox treading out the corn.

17. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE LAODICEANS. By the truth of the church, we hold this epistle sent to the Ephesians, not to the Laodiceans; but Marcion at some time desired to interpolate its title, as though he too were a most diligent investigator in this matter. But nothing turns on the titles, since the apostle wrote to all when he wrote to some — yet certainly preaching in Christ that God to whom belong the things that are preached. To whom, then, will they belong, according to the good pleasure which he set forth in the sacrament of his will, unto a dispensation of the fulfilment of the times (so to speak, as that word sounds in the Greek) to recapitulate — that is, to bring back to the beginning, or to review from the beginning — all things in Christ which are in the heavens and which are on earth — except him whose are all things from the beginning, even the very beginning, from which are both the times and the dispensation of the fulfilment of the times, on account of which all things are reviewed unto the beginning in Christ? But of another God what is the beginning — that is, the whence — whose work is none? what times without a beginning? what fulfilment without times? what dispensation without fulfilment? In short, what did he do on earth already of old, that any long dispensation of the times to be fulfilled should be reckoned, unto the reviewing of all things in Christ, even of those which are in the heavens? Nor shall we suppose that the things in the heavens, whatever they are, were wrought by another than by him by whom it is established that the things on earth too were wrought, by all consent. But if it cannot be that all these things are reckoned of another God from the beginning than the Creator, who will believe that they are reviewed by another unto another Christ, and not by their own author and unto his own Christ? If they are the Creator's, of necessity they must be diverse, since of a diverse God; if diverse, surely contrary. How then are contraries reviewed unto him by whom in the end they are destroyed? For also, what Christ do the following words announce, when he says, That we should be unto the praise of his glory, who first hoped in Christ? For who could have first hoped, that is, hoped before he came, in God, except the Jews, to whom Christ was foretold from the beginning? He, then, who was foretold was also first hoped in. And so this he refers to himself, that is, to the Jews, that he may make a distinction, turning to the nations: In whom you too, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel, in whom you believed and were sealed with the holy Spirit of his promise. Of what promise? made through Joel: In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh — that is, upon the nations too. So both the Spirit and the gospel will be in that Christ who was first hoped in, while he was being preached. But the Father of glory too is he whose Christ is sung the King of glory in the psalm, ascending: Who is this King of glory? the Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. From him is the Spirit of wisdom desired, with whom this species too of spiritual things is enumerated among the seven spirits through Isaiah. He will give the enlightened eyes of the heart who enriched the outward eyes too with light, who is displeased with the blindness of the people. And who is blind but my children? you are blinded, the servants of God. With him too are the riches of the inheritance in the saints, who promised that inheritance out of the calling of the nations. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance. He wrought in Christ his might, by raising him from the dead, and placing him at his right hand, and subjecting all things — who also said, Sit at my right hand, till I make your enemies the footstool of your feet; because also elsewhere the Spirit says to the Father concerning the Son, You have subjected all things under his feet. If from these things another God and another Christ are inferred, which are recognised in the Creator, let us now seek the Creator. Plainly, I think, we find him, when he says that those were dead in the offences in which they had walked, according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, who works in the sons of unbelief. But the world here too Marcion cannot interpret as the God of the world. For the made is not like the maker, the thing fashioned like the fashioner, the world like God. Nor will he be called the prince of the power of the air who is the prince of the power of the ages. For never is the president of the higher noted from the lower, though the lower too are reckoned to him. Nor can he be seen as the worker of unbelief, which he himself rather suffers both from the Jews and from the nations. It is enough, then, if these things do not fall upon the Creator. But if there is also one to whom they better befit, surely the apostle knew this the better. Who is he? Without doubt that one who obstructs against the Creator himself the sons of unbelief, having gained possession of this air, as the prophet reports him saying: I will set my throne in the clouds; I will be like the Most High. This will be the devil, whom elsewhere too (if indeed they will so have the apostle read) we shall acknowledge as the god of this age. For thus he has filled the whole world with the lie of his divinity. And plainly, if he had not been, then these things might have looked toward the Creator. But the apostle too had walked in Judaism. Not because he interposed about offences, in which we too all walked, is the Creator on that account to be understood the lord of offences and prince of this air; but because in Judaism he had been one of the sons of unbelief, having the devil as his worker, when he persecuted the church and Christ of the Creator — on which account too, We were, he says, children of wrath, but by nature. Lest, because the Creator called the Jews sons, the heretic argue from this that the Creator is the lord of wrath. For when he says, We were by nature children of wrath, but the Jews are not by nature the sons of the Creator, but by the election of the fathers, he referred the children of wrath to nature, not to the Creator — to sum it up, subjoining, As also the rest, who surely are not the sons of God. It appears that to the common nature of all men are reckoned both offences and the concupiscences of the flesh and unbelief and wrath, the devil nevertheless seizing upon nature, which he too has already infected by the seed of sin brought in. We are, he says, his workmanship, created in Christ. It is one thing to make, another to create; but he gave both to one. Now man is the workmanship of the Creator. The same, then, created in Christ who also made. For as far as concerns substance, he made; as far as concerns grace, he created. Look at the cohering words too. Remember that you were once nations in the flesh, who were called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand; that you were at that time without Christ, alienated from the converse of Israel and strangers to their testaments and promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. But without what God were the nations, and without what Christ? Surely him whose was the converse of Israel and the testaments and the promise. But now, he says, in Christ you who were far off are made near in his blood. From whom were they formerly far off? From those whom he names above: from the Christ of the Creator, from the converse of Israel, from the testaments, from the hope of the promise, from God himself. If these things are so, then the nations are now made near in Christ to those from whom they were then far off. But if to the converse of Israel, which is in the religion of God the Creator, and to the testaments — from God himself. If these things are so, then they are now made near, by calling, to those called from afar. They who were far from me have drawn near to my righteousness. For both the righteousness and the peace of the Creator were announced in Christ, as we have often already shown. And so, He himself, he says, is our peace, who made the two one — the Jewish people, namely, and the Gentile. The near and the far, the middle wall of enmity being dissolved, in his flesh. But Marcion took away His, that he might give the enmity to the flesh, as though to a carnal vice, not to a flesh hostile to Christ. Thus, as I said elsewhere, here too, not Marrucinian but Pontic, whose blood you confessed above, here you deny the flesh. If he made void the law of precepts by decrees — surely by fulfilling the law (for now there is no force in, You shall not commit adultery, when it is said, You shall not even look to lust; there is no force in, You shall not kill, when it is said, You shall not even curse) — he cannot make an adversary of the law out of one who assists it. That he might create the two in himself — who had made the same, creating (according to what is above too: We are his workmanship, created in Christ) — into one new man, making peace (if truly new, then truly a man too, not a phantasm; but new and newly — that is, newly born of a virgin by the Spirit of God) — that he might reconcile both to God, even to the God whom both kinds had offended, both the Jewish and the Gentile people, in one body, he says, having slain the enmity in it through the cross. So here too the flesh is the body in Christ, which could suffer the cross. This, then, announcing peace to those near and to those far, having obtained access together to the Father, we are now no longer strangers nor sojourners, but fellow-citizens of the saints, and of the household of God (surely of him from whom we showed above that we were aliens and set far off), built upon the foundation of the apostles. The heretic took away, And of the prophets, forgetting that the Lord set in the church, as apostles, so prophets too. He feared, namely, lest our building in Christ should stand even upon the foundations of the old prophets, since the apostle himself everywhere does not cease to build us up out of the prophets. For whence did he take to call Christ the chief cornerstone, except from the signification of the psalm: The stone which the builders rejected, the same is made into the head of the corner?

18. At the hands of the heretic who cuts away, I do not wonder if he withdraws syllables, when he very often subducts whole pages. The apostle, he says, was given grace, last of all, to enlighten all men as to what is the dispensation of the sacrament hidden from the ages in God, who created all things. The heretic snatched away the preposition In, and so makes it read: Hidden from the ages, to God who created all things. But the falsehood flashes out. For the apostle infers, That now there may be made known to the principalities and powers in the super-celestial places, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God. Of what principalities and powers does he speak? If the Creator's, what manner of thing is it that that God wished his wisdom to be shown to the Creator's principalities and powers, but not to himself — when the powers could not have known anything without their own prince? Or if for this reason he did not name God here, as though among them the prince himself too be reckoned, then he would have pronounced the sacrament hidden too from the principalities and powers of him who created all things, reckoning him likewise among them. But if he says it was hidden from them, to that one he ought to have said it was manifest. Therefore it was not hidden from God, but hidden in God the creator of all things, but hidden from his principalities and powers. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who was his counsellor? Here the heretic, caught, perhaps changed it to say that his God wished to make known to his own powers and principalities the dispensation of his sacrament, of which the God the founder of all things was ignorant. And how was it fitting to allege the ignorance of the Creator — a stranger and severed by long separation — when even the household members of the superior God did not know it? Yet to the Creator too it was to be known as future. Or was it not surely known, what under heaven and on earth, which were his, was to be revealed? Therefore from this is confirmed what we built above. For if the Creator was at some time to know that hidden sacrament of the superior God, and so the scripture ran, Hidden to God who created all things, he ought to have inferred thus: That there may be made known to him the manifold wisdom of God — then also to the powers and principalities of whatever God, with whom the Creator was to know it. So fully is it established that it was subtracted, which even so is safe to its own truth. I wish now too to weave a controversy with you about the apostle's allegories. What forms would he have had in the prophets, as one new? He led captivity captive, he says. With what arms? in what battles? from the laying waste of what nation? from the overthrow of what city? what women, what children, or what petty kings did he, as victor, bind in chains? For when in David Christ is sung as girded with a sword upon his thigh, or in Isaiah as receiving the spoils of Samaria and the strength of Damascus, you truly hammer him out a visible warrior too. Acknowledge, then, both his armour and his warfare to be spiritual, if you have already learned that there is a spiritual captivity, that you may acknowledge this too to be his — or because the apostle took the mention of this captivity too from the prophets, from whom too his commandments. Putting off lying, speak truth, each to his neighbour; and, Be angry and sin not (in the very words by which the psalm would expound his sense), let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Do not partake in the works of darkness. For with the just you shall be just, and with the perverse you shall be perverted; and, Take away evil from your midst; and, Go out from the midst of them; and, Touch not the unclean thing; be separate, you who bear the vessels of the Lord. So too, To be drunk with wine is unto disgrace — that is from the place where those who make the saints drunk are rebuked: And you gave my saints wine to drink; which both Aaron the priest and his sons were forbidden to drink, when they approached the holy things. And to sing to God in psalms and hymns and to teach is his who knew how to accuse before God those who drank wine to timbrels and psalteries. Thus, whose precepts and seeds of precepts or increments I find, his apostle I acknowledge. For the rest, whence does he confirm that women ought to be subject to men? Because the man, he says, is the head of the woman. Tell me, Marcion: from a work of the Creator does your God lend authority to his own law? This now is plainly the lesser thing, since both for his own Christ and for his church he takes a status from there, just as Christ too is the head of the church. Likewise too, when he says, He who loves his own wife loves his own flesh, just as Christ too the church. You see your Christ and your church compared to a work of the Creator. How much honour is given to the flesh in the name of the church! Let no one, he says, hate his own flesh (except plainly Marcion alone), but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ too the church. But you alone hate it, taking away from it the resurrection. You ought to hate the church too, because it is likewise loved by Christ. But indeed Christ loved the flesh too, just as the church. No one but loves even the image of his bride; nay, he will both preserve and honour and crown it. The likeness has a partnership of honour with the truth. I shall now labour to prove the same God of the male and of Christ, of the woman and of the church, of the flesh and of the spirit, since the apostle himself adduces — nay, expounds — the sentence of the Creator: For this cause a man shall leave father and mother, and the two shall be in one flesh. This is a great sacrament. It is enough among these things if the Creator's sacraments are great with the apostle, the least with the heretics. But I, he says, speak of Christ and the church. He has an interpretation, not a separation, of the sacrament. He shows the figure of the sacrament to have been furnished beforehand by him whose surely the sacrament was. What seems to Marcion? The Creator surely could not furnish figures beforehand to an unknown God — and even, if known, to an adversary. The superior God ought to have borrowed nothing from the inferior, and that rather unto destruction. Let children too obey their parents. For though Marcion took away, This is the first precept in promise, the law speaks, Honour father and mother; and, Parents, bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord. For you have heard it said to the ancients too, You shall tell these things in the ears of your children, and your children likewise in the ears of their children. Why now do you give me two gods, if the discipline is one? And if there are two, I will follow him who first taught. But if our wrestling is against the world-holders — O how many gods the Creators already are! For why should I not vindicate this too — that one world-holder ought to have been named, if it signified the Creator, whose were those powers which he set before? Further, since above he bids us put on the armour in which we may stand against the machinations of the devil, he now shows that those things are the devil's which he subjoins to the devil — the powers and world-holders of these darknesses, which we too reckon to the devil. Or if the devil is the Creator, who will be the devil with the Creator? Or, as there are two gods, so two devils too, and, in the plural, powers and world-holders? But how is the Creator both devil and God, when the devil is not himself both God and devil? For either both are gods too, if both are now devils; or he who is God here and not devil, just as the devil is not God. The very word devil — I ask of what accusation it can befit the Creator. Perhaps he carried off some plan of the superior God — which the Creator himself suffered from the archangel, and that one lying. For he had not forbidden the taste of that little tree lest they should become gods, but lest they should die of the transgression. Nor did the spiritual wickednesses signify the Creator because he added, In the heavens. For the apostle too knew that spiritual wickednesses had been wrought in the heavens — of the angels that gave offence with the daughters of men. And what manner of thing was it that by ambiguities and through riddles I know not what he should tax the Creator — he who, set already in chains for the liberty of his preaching, was begging from God constancy in manifesting the sacrament by the opening of his mouth, which there he was bidding to be demanded of God, and surely furnishing it for the church?

19. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. In my prescription against all heresies I am wont to fix a compendium from the testimony of the times, vindicating our rule as prior to all heretical posterity. This now the apostle too will prove, saying, Of the hope laid up in the heavens, which you heard in the word of the truth of the gospel, which has come to you, just as into the whole world too. For if even then the evangelic tradition had spread everywhere, how much more now? Further, if ours is that which has spread everywhere, more than any heretical thing, much less the Antoninian Marcion's, it will be ours, apostolic. But Marcion's, though it have filled the whole world, will not even then be able to defend itself as apostolic. For that will even so be established to be apostolic which first filled the world — namely, with the gospel of that God who sang this too of his preachings: Into all the earth their sound has gone out, and into the ends of the world their words. He says Christ is the image of the invisible God. But we too call the Father of Christ invisible, knowing that the Son was always seen of old, if to any he was seen under the name of God, as his image — lest from this too he split off some difference of a visible and an invisible God, since of old the definition of our God has been, No one shall see God and live. If Christ is not the firstborn of creation, as the Word of the Creator through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made; if in him were not created all things that are in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; if all things were not created through him and in him (for these things Marcion ought to have been displeased at) — surely the apostle would not have set it down so nakedly, And he is before all. For how before all, if not before all things? How before all things, if not the firstborn of creation, if not the Word of the Creator? Whence shall he be proved to have been before all, who appeared after all things? Who knows that one to have been prior whom he did not know to be at all? How likewise did he think good that all fullness should dwell in himself? For first, what is this fullness, except out of those things which Marcion took away — created in Christ, in the heavens and on earth, angels and men — except out of those invisible and visible things, except out of thrones and dominions and principalities and powers? Or if our pseudo-apostles and Jewish evangelisers brought these in of their own, and to the fullness of his God, Marcion, who created nothing — for the rest, what manner of thing is it that the rival and destroyer of the Creator should have wished the Creator's fullness to dwell in his own Christ? To whom, in short, does he reconcile all things unto himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, except him whom these same things had offended, against whom they had rebelled by transgression, whose at the last they had been? For they could be conciliated to a stranger, but reconciled to no other than their own. So too us, once alienated and enemies in mind in evil works, he reduces into grace with the Creator, whose offence we had committed, worshipping the creation against the Creator. But if anywhere too he says the church is the body of Christ — as here he says that he fills up the remnants of the tribulations of Christ in his flesh for his body, which is the church — you will not on that account transfer the mention of the body wholly from the substance of the flesh. For above too he says that we are reconciled in his body through death — surely in that body in which he could die, through the flesh he died, not through the church, but plainly for the church, exchanging body for body, the carnal for the spiritual. But when he warns us to beware of subtle speech and philosophy, as of vain seduction which is according to the elements of the world — not speaking of heaven or earth, but of secular letters and tradition, namely of subtle-speaking men and philosophers — it is a long matter, indeed, and of another work, to show that by this sentence all heresies are condemned, because all consist of the resources of subtle speech and the rules of philosophy. But let Marcion acknowledge the chief boundary of his faith from the school of Epicurus, bringing in a dull lord, that he may say he is not to be feared; placing too matter, with God the Creator, from the porch of the Stoics; denying the resurrection of the flesh, on which likewise no philosophy agrees. From whose ingenuities our truth is so far removed, that it both dreads to rouse the wrath of God, and trusts that he brought forth all things out of nothing, and promises that he will restore the same flesh, and does not blush at a Christ born from a virgin's womb — though the philosophers and heretics and the very heathen laugh. For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise — he, without doubt, who out of regard for this his arrangement threatened beforehand that he would destroy the wisdom of the wise. By this simplicity of truth, contrary to subtle speech and philosophy, we can savour nothing perverse. In short, if God makes us alive with Christ, forgiving us our offences, we cannot believe that offences are forgiven by him against whom they were not committed, as one formerly unknown. Come now, when he says, Let no one judge you in food and drink, or in part of a feast-day or a new moon or a sabbath, which is a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's — what seems to you, Marcion? Of the law we now do not treat again, except that here too he teaches in what manner it has been excluded, while, namely, it is transferred from the shadow to the body — that is, from figures to the truth, which is Christ. Therefore the shadow too is his whose is the body — that is, both the law is his and Christ. Separate the law to one God and Christ to another, if you can separate any shadow from the body of which it is the shadow. Manifestly Christ is of the law, if he is the body of the shadow. But if he also taxes some who out of angelic visions said that food must be abstained from — Touch not, taste not — wishing to walk in the lowliness of sense, not holding the head — not on that account does he assail the law and Moses, as though out of angelic superstition he had appointed the interdiction of certain foods. For it is established that Moses received the law from God. In short, this discipline — According to the precepts, he says, and doctrine of men — he reckoned upon those who held not the head, that is, him in whom all things are reviewed, brought back to the beginning in Christ — even the indifference of foods. The rest of the precepts — that it may suffice to have already taught elsewhere whence they flowed from the Creator, who, when he preached that the old things would pass, about to make all things new, commanding too, Make for yourselves a new renewal, even then was teaching to put off the old man and put on the new.
