20. ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS. When he enumerates the variety of preaching — that some, from the confidence of his chains, uttered the word more boldly, others through envy and contention, certain through esteem of the discourse, very many out of love, some out of emulation, now some too out of strife, preached Christ — there was surely here a place too for taxing the very preaching, on the diversity of sentence which made so great a variety even of dispositions. But, setting forth in the diversity the causes only of dispositions, not the rules of the sacraments, he confirms that one Christ nevertheless, and one God of his, was preached, whatever the intent; and therefore, It is nothing to me, he says, whether by occasion or in truth Christ is announced, because one was announced, whether out of occasion or out of the truth of faith. For he referred the mention of truth to the faith of the preaching, not to the rule itself, because the rule indeed was one, but the faith of certain preachers was true, that is, simple, of certain over-learned. Since this is so, it appears that the Christ preached was he who was always announced. For if another, far from the apostle, were brought in, the newness of the thing would have made a diversity. For there would not have been wanting those who would nonetheless interpret the evangelic preaching as of the Christ of the Creator, since even today the greater part in all places is of our sentence than of the heretical. So that here too the apostle would not have been silent about noting and rebuking the diversity. Thus, since the diversity is not even taxed, the newness is not proved. Plainly the Marcionites think that here too the apostle votes for them about the substance of Christ — that there was a phantasm of flesh in Christ — when he says that, being constituted in the form of God, he counted it not robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not the truth, and in the likeness of man, not in man, and being found in fashion as man, not in substance, that is, not in flesh — as though fashion and likeness and form did not accrue to substance too. But well that elsewhere too he calls Christ the image of the invisible God. Surely, then, here too, in that he sets him in the form of God, will Christ likewise not be truly God, if not truly man too, being constituted in the form of man? For both ways the truth will have to be excluded, if fashion and likeness and form be claimed for a phantasm. But if in form and in image, in which he is the Son of the Father, he is truly God, it is prejudged that in the form and image too of man, in which he is the Son of man, he was found truly man. For he set down found with reason, that is, most certainly man. For what is found is established to be. So too God was found through power, as man through flesh, because he would not have pronounced one subject to death who was not constituted in mortal substance. But more is what he added, And the death of the cross. For he would not have heightened the atrocity by extolling the might of the subjection, had he known it imaginary, by a phantasm — rather frustrated than experienced, nor discharging any might in the passion, but in mockery. But the things which formerly he had reckoned gain, which above too he enumerates — the glory of the flesh, the mark of circumcision, the reckoning of Hebrew race out of a Hebrew, the title of the tribe of Benjamin, the dignity of pure Pharisaism — these now he reckons to himself for loss; not God, but the stupor of the Jews. These he counts but as dung, in comparison with the knowledge of Christ, not in rejection of God the Creator; having a righteousness not now his own, which is of the law, but that which is through him, namely Christ, of God. Therefore, you say, by this distinction the law was not of the God of Christ. Subtly enough. Receive, then, more subtly. For when he says, Not that which is of the law, but that which is through him, he would not have said Through him of another than him whose the law was. Our citizenship, he says, is in the heavens. I recognise the old promise of the Creator to Abraham: And I will make your seed as the stars in heaven. Therefore too star differs from star in glory. But if Christ, coming from the heavens, transfigured the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory, then this our body shall rise, which is humbled in sufferings, and cast into the earth by the very law of death. For how shall it be transfigured, if it shall be nothing? Or if it is said of those who, found in the flesh at the coming of God, are to be reckoned, what shall they do who first rise? They will have nothing out of which to be transfigured. But, We shall be caught up, he says, together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord. If caught up together with them, surely transfigured too together with them.

21. ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON. To this epistle alone its brevity was of profit, that it might escape the falsifying hands of Marcion. Yet I wonder that, when he received letters written to one man, he rejected the two to Timothy and the one to Titus, composed about ecclesiastical order. He affected, I think, to interpolate even the number of the epistles. Remember, inspector, that the things which were treated beforehand we have proved of the apostle too in their place, and that whatever was deferred to this work we have discharged — lest either here you think the iteration superfluous, by which we have confirmed the former hope, or there hold the deferment suspect, by which we drew out these very things. If you inspect the whole little work, you will judge neither here a redundance nor there a diffidence.
